sessions.goal: Do 30 push-ups in a row within 8 weeks. I can do about 8 rig

protocol.goal_statement: Go from ~8 clean push-ups to 30 unbroken in 8 weeks, training 4 mornings a week at home.

phases.title: Build the base
phases.focus: Four short morning sessions a week, every set stopped with 2-3 reps still in the tank. Nothing near failure — volume is the whole point right now.

steps.title: Monday & Thursday push-up session
steps.details: 5 sets of 5 reps, 90 seconds rest between sets. Stop each set with 2-3 clean reps still in you — if rep 5 gets grindy, drop to 4 next set. Two light warm-up sets of 5 first. Do it on the floor in the same spot each time.

how_to.gist: 5 sets of 5, 90 seconds rest, stopping 2-3 reps short of failure.
how_to.why: Your max is around 8, so sets of 5 are easy enough to repeat four times a week without wrecking you — and the total reps per week is what actually moves your number up.

sections.heading: The session
items: 2 light warm-up sets of 5, easy pace
5 working sets of 5 reps
90 seconds rest between every set
Stop each set with 2-3 reps still in the tank

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: If the last rep of a set slows down or your hips sag, that set is over — cut it to 4 and keep going. Grinding out a shaky rep today costs you Thursday's session.

sections.heading: Where
sections.body: Same spot on the floor every time, first thing before the day starts. Leave nothing to decide in the morning.

how_to.counts_as_done: 5 working sets of 5 completed, any order, no set taken to failure.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: 5x5. Week 3: 5x6 if every set of week 2 felt clean.

steps.title: Tuesday & Friday push-up session
steps.details: A different flavour from Monday: 4 sets, each one stopping 3 reps short of your best. If your best is 8, that's sets of 5 — but with only 60 seconds rest, so it's harder than it looks. Two light warm-up sets first.

how_to.gist: 4 sets of 5 with only 60 seconds rest — shorter rest, same easy reps.
how_to.why: Shorter rest builds the endurance you'll need for one long unbroken set later, without ever pushing a single set to failure.

Stop 3 reps short of your best

sections.heading: If it gets hard
sections.body: Add 15 seconds of rest rather than cutting reps. The reps stay clean; only the clock moves.

sections.heading: Why short rest
sections.body: Doing 30 in a row is one long effort. Training with less recovery teaches your muscles to keep going while they're still tired.

how_to.counts_as_done: 4 working sets completed with 60 seconds rest, no set to failure.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: 4x5 at 60s rest. Week 3: 4x6 at 60s rest.

steps.title: Write down every set
steps.details: Right after each session, note the sets and reps you actually did and how the last rep of each set felt. Next session, beat one number — one extra rep on one set is enough. This is the only thing that tells you the plan is working before week 4.

how_to.gist: Note your sets and reps after each session, then beat one number next time.
how_to.why: Push-up progress stalls when you can't tell whether last week was harder or easier. One line per session turns guesswork into a direction.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Next session, beat one number — one extra rep on one set, or the same reps with cleaner form. Never chase two at once.

sections.heading: Where
sections.body: Notes app, notebook, whiteboard by the door. Anywhere you'll see it before the next session.

how_to.counts_as_done: A written note exists for that session, with at least one number to beat.

steps.week_progression: Same habit all the way through — the numbers you're beating get bigger.

steps.title: Hit ~150 g protein a day
steps.details: Roughly 150 g of protein across the day — a palm-sized portion at each of your three meals, plus a shake or a tub of Greek yoghurt to close the gap. You're asking your chest and arms to get stronger four mornings a week; this is what they rebuild with.

how_to.gist: About 150 g of protein a day, spread across your meals.
how_to.why: Training four mornings a week only pays off if your body has something to rebuild with. Around 150 g a day is the amount that matches your bodyweight.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: About 150 g a day. That's a palm-sized protein portion at each of three meals, plus one extra — a shake, a pot of Greek yoghurt, a couple of eggs.

sections.body: One low day is noise. Two in a row during a training week is when the reps start feeling heavier than they should.

how_to.counts_as_done: Roughly 150 g of protein eaten, spread over the day.

steps.week_progression: Same target throughout. If meals are already solid, this is a five-second check, not a change.

steps.title: Lights out by 11pm
steps.details: In bed with the lights off by 11pm, phone charging across the room. Four morning sessions only work if you're actually recovered for them — and the morning alarm is what makes the bedtime non-negotiable.

how_to.gist: Lights off by 11pm, phone charging in another room.
how_to.why: Your sessions are at the front of the day, so a late night doesn't cost you an evening — it costs you the session. Recovery is where the strength actually gets built.

steps.title: Week 4 max test
steps.details: One all-out set, fresh, after a rest day. Stop the moment your form breaks — hips sagging or reps getting shorter means the set is over. Write the number down. This is the only max attempt between now and week 8.

how_to.gist: One all-out set on Saturday, stop when form breaks, write the number down.
how_to.why: You need one honest checkpoint in the middle so you know whether the volume is working — and so you don't spend weeks guessing.

protocol.coach_notes: The first 15 reps come quickly and the last 5 are a grind — that's normal, not a sign you've stalled. The one rule that matters: never miss two sessions in a row. One missed morning is noise; the session after the miss is the one that decides whether this habit survives. And don't test your max between the scheduled checkpoints — the temptation to see if you're 'there yet' is what kills this plan for most people.

sessions.goal: Read a lot more this year — I keep buying books and not read

protocol.goal_statement: Read 10 pages in bed at 10:30 on weeknights, phone charging in the kitchen overnight, plus one audiobook chapter on the Saturday walk
protocol.short_title: Read 10 pages a night for 12 weeks

phases.title: Get the phone out of the room
phases.focus: Ten pages at 10:30 on weeknights, phone charging in the kitchen, one audiobook chapter on the Saturday walk. Nothing else changes yet.

steps.title: 10 pages in bed at 10:30
steps.details: Book in hand at 10:30, ten pages before anything else. Any book, any pace — ten pages is about fifteen minutes. If you're still awake after ten, keep going; if you're not, close it and sleep.

how_to.gist: Book open at 10:30, ten pages read before you do anything else.
how_to.why: This is the whole plan. Ten pages a night is roughly fifteen minutes, and fifteen minutes a night is a book every few weeks — which is the difference between buying books and reading them.

sections.heading: The setup
sections.body: Book on the nightstand, phone already in the kitchen. At 10:30 you pick up the book, not the phone. Read in bed, lights on, however you're comfortable.

sections.heading: The ten pages
sections.body: Ten pages, any pace. Slow is fine. If you're enjoying it at page ten, keep going — the ten is a floor, not a ceiling. If you're falling asleep at page six, read to ten anyway and then sleep; the point is the ten, not the chapter.

sections.heading: When it's late
sections.body: If you get home at 11, you still read ten pages. It's fifteen minutes. The only night you skip is a night you're not in bed at all.

how_to.counts_as_done: Ten pages read, in bed, on that night.

steps.title: Phone charges in the kitchen overnight
steps.details: Phone goes on the kitchen charger when you start getting ready for bed and stays there until morning. Alarm clock or watch in the bedroom instead — whatever you need to wake up, it isn't the phone.

how_to.gist: Phone on the kitchen charger before bed, and it stays there till morning.
how_to.why: The phone within arm's reach at 10:30 is the exact thing that's been beating you — you said yourself you drift to it. Take it out of the room and the ten pages get a fair fight.

sections.heading: When
sections.body: The moment you start getting ready for bed, not when you get into bed. If it's still in your pocket at 10:30, the reading loses.

sections.heading: What wakes you up
sections.body: Set an alarm clock or wear a watch. If you genuinely need the phone alarm, set it before you park the phone and leave it in the kitchen — you'll get up to turn it off, which is a bonus.

sections.heading: The one exception
sections.body: If someone in your life needs to reach you overnight, tell them to call the landline or ring twice. Otherwise, no exceptions — a phone that comes back to the bedroom at 11 is a phone that's back for good.

how_to.counts_as_done: Phone on the kitchen charger when you went to bed, and still there in the morning.

steps.title: One audiobook chapter on the Saturday walk
steps.details: Headphones in on the Saturday walk, one chapter of an audiobook. This is the easy one — it's a walk you were taking anyway, and it's the reset button for a week that went sideways.

how_to.gist: One audiobook chapter, headphones in, on your Saturday walk.
how_to.why: A second, easier way in. When weeknights go badly — and some will — Saturday is a win you can still bank, and it keeps the week from being a total loss.

sections.heading: The walk
sections.body: Whatever walk you already take on Saturday. Chapter on from the moment you step out. If the chapter ends before you're home, that's fine — one chapter is the target.

sections.heading: If the week was rough
sections.body: If you only read one or two nights that week, this walk is the reset. Do the chapter, then start the next week fresh on Monday. One bad week doesn't end anything.

how_to.counts_as_done: One chapter finished on the Saturday walk.

steps.title: Three nights is a bad week, not a lost one
steps.details: This one exists because your last reading goal died in week two when work got busy, and nothing in the plan said what to do about it. So here it is in advance: a week where you read three nights is a week you held. Four or five is a good week. Zero is the only number that ends the habit — and even then, the Saturday walk is your way back in.

how_to.gist: Three nights of reading in a week counts as holding the line.
how_to.why: Last year's attempt died in week two when work got busy, because a missed night felt like a verdict. Naming the bad-week minimum now means a brutal Tuesday can't end the plan.

sections.heading: The numbers
items: Five nights — a full week, nothing to think about
Four nights — a good week
Three nights — a bad week, and you're still in it
Two or fewer — do the Saturday chapter, then start again Monday

sections.heading: The rule that matters
sections.body: Never miss two nights in a row. One missed night is noise. The night after a miss is the one that decides whether this is a habit or a memory.

sections.heading: If work eats a week
sections.body: Read three nights, do the Saturday chapter, and carry on. Don't restart the count, don't add pages to make up for it, don't re-plan. Just take the next Monday.

how_to.counts_as_done: At least three nights of reading in the week, or the Saturday chapter done as the reset.

phases.title: Make 10:30 the default
phases.focus: Same plan, but the start time moves earlier and the pages go up a little. The phone rule stops being a rule and becomes just where the phone lives.

steps.title: 12 pages in bed at 10:15
steps.details: Two more pages, fifteen minutes earlier. By now ten pages should feel routine, so this is a small step up, not a new plan. Same book, same bed, same rule about late nights.
steps.week_progression: Start time moves from 10:30 to 10:15 and the floor goes from 10 pages to 12.

steps.details: Unchanged. Phone on the kitchen charger before you start getting ready for bed, alarm clock in the bedroom, phone still there in the morning.
steps.week_progression: No change — this is the step that should now be automatic.

steps.title: One audiobook chapter on the Saturday walk
steps.details: Unchanged. One chapter on the Saturday walk, and the reset button if the week went sideways.
steps.week_progression: No change.

steps.title: Three nights is a bad week, not a lost one
steps.details: Unchanged, and it matters more now that the target is higher. Three nights holds the line. Never miss two in a row. The Saturday chapter is the way back.
steps.week_progression: No change.

steps.title: Finish one book
steps.details: This one is here because reading ten pages a night and never finishing anything is how a shelf of half-read books happens. Pick the book you're closest to finishing and get to the last page. Then start the next one the same night.

how_to.gist: Get to the last page of one book, then start the next one that night.
how_to.why: You said you keep buying books and not reading them. Finishing one is the proof that this is working — and starting the next one the same night is what stops the gap that becomes a month off.

sections.heading: Which book
sections.body: Whichever one you're furthest into. Don't start something new to avoid finishing something old.

sections.heading: The same night rule
sections.body: The night you finish, you open the next book and read your pages in it. A finished book with nothing after it is where reading habits go to die.

how_to.counts_as_done: A book reached its last page, and the next one was opened the same night.

phases.title: Reading without the scaffolding
phases.focus: The pages go up again and the Saturday chapter becomes optional — because by now you read on weeknights without needing a rescue plan.

steps.title: 15 pages in bed at 10:15
steps.details: Fifteen pages, still at 10:15. That's roughly twenty minutes and about a book a month. Same rules: late nights still count, ten pages on a bad night still counts as a night.
steps.week_progression: Floor goes from 12 pages to 15.

steps.title: Phone charges in the kitchen overnight
steps.details: Unchanged. This should be where the phone lives now, not a rule you're following.
steps.week_progression: No change.

steps.title: Saturday audiobook — your call
steps.details: The Saturday chapter is now optional. If you want it, take it. If weeknights are solid and you'd rather listen to music on the walk, that's a sign the plan worked, not a sign you're slacking.
steps.week_progression: Changes from required to optional — it's done its job as the safety net.

steps.title: Three nights is a bad week, not a lost one
steps.details: Still here, and it stays here. Three nights holds the line, never miss two in a row, and a rough week is not a reason to re-plan anything.
steps.week_progression: No change.

steps.title: Finish two more books
steps.details: Two more books finished before the twelve weeks are up. Same rule as before: the night you finish one, you start the next.
steps.week_progression: From one book finished to two more.

milestones.title: Four weeks in — past where last year's attempt died
milestones.criteria: Four consecutive weeks where you read at least three nights, with the phone in the kitchen every night.

milestones.title: One book finished, and 10:15 feels normal
milestones.criteria: A book reached its last page and the next one opened the same night, plus four more weeks of at least three reading nights.

milestones.title: Three books read, and reading is just what you do at night
milestones.criteria: Three books finished across the twelve weeks, and the last four weeks held at three or more reading nights without needing the Saturday chapter as a rescue.

protocol.coach_notes: You built this plan yourself, and that's not a small thing — the phone in the kitchen is the move that actually matters here, and you got there on your own. The only thing I added is the floor: three nights is a bad week, not a lost one, because a busy week in week two is exactly what killed the last attempt and now it has a script. One missed night is noise. The night after a miss is the one that decides this — take it, and you're still in.

sessions.goal: Lose 10 lbs

protocol.goal_statement: Lose 10 lbs (about 4.5 kg) with daily walks, two gym sessions a week, and a simple protein-and-portion rule at meals

phases.title: Start where you already are
phases.focus: Get the walk in every day, get to the gym twice, and run the three food rules without counting anything.

steps.title: Daily walk, 20 minutes
steps.details: Twenty minutes outside, at a pace where you could still hold a conversation. Same time each day — the one that already has a gap in it. Weekday version can be a loop from the office door; weekend version can be longer if you feel like it, but twenty is the bar.

how_to.gist: Twenty minutes outside, every day, at a pace you could talk through.
how_to.why: This is the cheapest thing in the plan and the one that carries the most weight. It burns a little, it keeps you out of the kitchen, and it's the habit that survives a bad week.

sections.heading: The walk
sections.body: Twenty minutes, outside, at a pace where you could still hold a conversation. Not a march, not a stroll — the pace you'd walk if you were five minutes late for something but didn't want to arrive sweaty.

sections.heading: When
sections.body: Pick the slot that already exists in your day and keep it there. Lunch break, right after work, before dinner — whichever one you'd actually defend. Same slot every day beats a better slot you only use twice.

sections.heading: If it's awful out
sections.body: Go anyway, shorter. Ten minutes in the rain still counts as the walk; skipping it because the weather's bad is how the streak dies in week two.

how_to.counts_as_done: Twenty minutes of walking, logged, on the day it happened.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: 20 minutes. Weeks 3-4: 25 minutes if 20 has felt easy every day.

steps.title: Two gym sessions
steps.details: Full-body both days: a squat or leg press, a push, a pull, a hip hinge, and one carry or core movement. Three sets of 8-12 reps each, 2-3 light warm-up sets before your first working set. Tuesday and Friday, or whatever two days you'll actually keep — they should not be back-to-back.

how_to.gist: Two full-body sessions a week, three sets of 8-12 on five movements.
how_to.why: Two sessions is enough to tell your body to keep its muscle while the scale moves. Lose weight without lifting and some of what goes is the muscle you'd rather keep.

sections.heading: The five movements
items: Squat or leg press
A push — bench press, dumbbell press, or push-up
A pull — row or lat pulldown
A hip hinge — deadlift or Romanian deadlift
A carry or core — farmer's carry, plank, or hanging knee raise

sections.heading: Sets and reps
sections.body: Three sets of 8-12 reps on each. Pick a weight where the last two reps of the last set are genuinely hard but you're not grinding to failure. Two or three light warm-up sets before your first working set on each movement.

sections.heading: The days
sections.body: Tuesday and Friday, or any two days that aren't back-to-back. Same two days every week — the point is that you stop deciding.

how_to.counts_as_done: Both sessions done this week, any order, any time of day.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: learn the movements, keep the weight light. Weeks 3-4: add a little weight or a rep whenever the last set felt manageable.

steps.title: Write down every set
steps.details: Note the weight and reps for each set in your phone as you go. Next session, your job is to beat one thing — one more rep, or 2.5 kg more on your main lift. Same numbers twice in a row means it's time to add something.

how_to.gist: Log each set, then beat one number next time you're in.
how_to.why: Without this, the gym becomes a place you visit rather than a place that changes you. Two sessions a week only holds your muscle if the sessions are getting slightly harder over time.

sections.heading: What to write
sections.body: Weight and reps for each set, in your phone, as you do them. Nothing fancy — '60 x 10, 60 x 9, 60 x 8' is a complete entry.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Before each session, look at last time's numbers and pick one to beat. One more rep on any set, or 2.5 kg more on your main lift. That's the whole job.

sections.heading: When it stalls
sections.body: If the same numbers show up twice in a row, add a small amount of weight and let the reps drop — then build them back up.

how_to.counts_as_done: Both sessions have numbers written down, and you beat at least one of them.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: just get the habit of writing. Weeks 3-4: beating one number per session becomes the standard.

steps.title: Protein at every meal
steps.details: Roughly 130 g of protein a day, spread across your meals rather than saved for dinner. A palm-sized portion of meat, fish, eggs, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, beans or tofu at breakfast, lunch and dinner gets you most of the way there.

how_to.gist: A palm-sized protein portion at breakfast, lunch and dinner.
how_to.why: Protein is what keeps you full between meals and what protects your muscle while you lose weight. It's the one food rule that does two jobs at once.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: About 130 g a day, worked out from the weight range you gave me. You don't need to count it precisely — three palm-sized portions across the day plus a protein-heavy snack gets you there.

sections.heading: What counts
items: Meat, chicken, fish — a palm-sized piece
Eggs — two or three
Greek yogurt or cottage cheese — a big bowl
Beans, lentils, tofu — a fist-sized portion
A scoop of protein powder in milk or water

sections.heading: The easy fix
sections.body: Breakfast is usually where this falls apart. If you normally eat toast or cereal, add eggs or a yogurt to it rather than replacing it — that alone is often 25-30 g.

how_to.counts_as_done: Three meals with a real protein portion in each.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: get protein into breakfast. Weeks 3-4: all three meals, most days.

steps.title: One plate, kitchen closed after dinner
steps.details: One plate at dinner, no going back for seconds, and nothing to eat after dinner is over. Water, tea or coffee are fine afterwards — food isn't. This is the rule that does the work on the days the walk and the gym can't.

how_to.gist: One plate at dinner, then the kitchen is closed for the night.
how_to.why: Late-night eating is where a good day quietly turns into a flat week. This rule costs you nothing at breakfast or lunch and takes back the hours where the extra food actually lives.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Serve dinner once, eat it, and that's the meal. No seconds, no standing at the counter afterwards, no bowl of something while you watch TV.

sections.heading: After dinner
sections.body: Water, tea or coffee are fine. If you want something sweet, have it as part of dinner rather than an hour later — same food, different habit.

sections.heading: If you're actually hungry
sections.body: If dinner genuinely didn't fill you, add more protein and vegetables to the plate next time rather than eating again later. That's the fix, not willpower at 10pm.

how_to.counts_as_done: One plate at dinner and nothing to eat afterwards.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: hit this four or five nights out of seven. Weeks 3-4: most nights.

steps.title: In bed by 11pm
steps.details: Lights out by 11pm, aiming for seven to eight hours. Short sleep makes you hungrier the next day and makes the gym feel heavier than it is — this is a weight-loss step, not a wellness footnote.

how_to.gist: Lights out by 11pm, seven to eight hours of sleep.
how_to.why: Sleep is the step nobody connects to the scale, and it's one of the strongest ones. Tired people eat more and train worse — you'll feel the difference in the gym within a week.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: In bed, lights out, by 11pm. Seven to eight hours. Pick the bedtime that gets you there and work backwards from your alarm.

sections.heading: The run-up
sections.body: Phone on the charger across the room half an hour before bed. That's the whole trick — most late nights are a screen, not a decision.

sections.heading: If you miss it
sections.body: One late night is nothing. Two in a row is when the snacking and the skipped walks start showing up.

how_to.counts_as_done: Lights out by 11pm.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: aim for five nights out of seven. Weeks 3-4: most nights.

phases.title: Build the habit into a routine
phases.focus: Longer walks, heavier gym sessions, and the food rules running without you having to think about them.

steps.title: Daily walk, 30 minutes
steps.details: Thirty minutes now, same slot as before. If thirty feels like a lot on a given day, go twenty — the streak matters more than the extra ten minutes.

how_to.gist: Same walk, ten minutes longer.
how_to.why: The walk is the lever that moves the scale most reliably for you, and thirty minutes is where it starts to matter without eating into your day.

sections.heading: The change
sections.body: Thirty minutes instead of twenty, same time, same route. Nothing else about it changes.

sections.heading: The floor
sections.body: On a bad day, twenty minutes still counts as the walk. Don't let a perfect thirty become a skipped zero.

how_to.counts_as_done: Thirty minutes of walking, logged.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-6: 30 minutes. Weeks 7-8: 35 minutes if it's been easy.

steps.title: Two gym sessions, heavier
steps.details: Same five movements, same two days. The difference now is the weight: every session should have at least one set that's harder than anything you did in week one. Add 2.5 kg to your main lift whenever you hit the top of the rep range on all three sets.

how_to.gist: Same two sessions, but the weights are climbing.
how_to.why: Weeks 1-4 taught your body the movements. From here the sessions have to get harder or they stop doing anything — this is the phase where the gym starts protecting your muscle for real.

sections.heading: How to add
sections.body: When you hit 12 reps on all three sets of a movement, add 2.5 kg next time and let the reps drop back to 8. Build them up again.

sections.heading: The check
sections.body: Once a session, look at your log and make sure something in it is heavier or longer than a month ago. If nothing is, add weight to your main lift that day.

how_to.counts_as_done: Both sessions done, with at least one set heavier than week one.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-6: add weight on the main lift. Weeks 7-8: add weight on a second movement too.

steps.title: Write down every set
steps.details: Same logbook habit, now with a target: beat last session's numbers on at least one set. Two sessions in a row with identical numbers means add weight.

how_to.gist: Log every set and beat one number from last time.
how_to.why: This is the step that turns two gym visits into actual progress. It's also the first thing to slip when life gets busy, so it stays its own job.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Numbers in your phone as you go. Before you start, pick one number from last session to beat.

sections.heading: The stall rule
sections.body: Same numbers twice in a row? Add 2.5 kg and rebuild the reps.

how_to.counts_as_done: Both sessions logged, one number beaten.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-8: beating one number per session is the standard, not the bonus.

steps.title: Protein at every meal
steps.details: Same 130 g target, now with a second look at portions. If the scale has been flat, the protein isn't the problem — the plate size is. Keep the protein, tighten the rest.

how_to.gist: 130 g of protein a day, three meals, no skipping.
how_to.why: By now this should be automatic. Keeping it steady is what stops the weight coming off your muscle instead of your waist.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: About 130 g, spread across three meals. A palm-sized portion each time.

sections.heading: If the scale stalls
sections.body: Don't cut protein. Cut the extras around it — the second helping, the snack, the drink. Protein is the last thing to touch.

how_to.counts_as_done: Three protein portions, three meals.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-8: same target, tighter portions if the scale has gone flat.

steps.title: One plate, kitchen closed after dinner
steps.details: Same rule, and by now it should be the default rather than a decision. If you've had a couple of weeks where the scale didn't move, this is the rule to look at first.

how_to.gist: One plate at dinner, nothing to eat afterwards.
how_to.why: This is the rule that quietly does the most work. It's also the first one to bend when you're tired, so it stays visible.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: One plate at dinner. Water, tea or coffee afterwards — no food.

sections.heading: If it's slipping
sections.body: Move dinner half an hour later rather than adding a snack before bed. Same calories, better habit.

how_to.counts_as_done: One plate, kitchen closed.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-8: most nights, without thinking about it.

steps.title: In bed by 11pm
steps.details: Same bedtime. In this phase the gym sessions are getting heavier, and that only works if you're sleeping. A short night shows up as a bad session two days later.

how_to.gist: Lights out by 11pm.
how_to.why: Heavier training needs more recovery, not less. Sleep is where the sessions actually turn into kept muscle.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: Lights out by 11pm, seven to eight hours.

sections.heading: The tell
sections.body: If a session feels unusually heavy and you slept badly two nights before, that's the connection. Fix the sleep, not the workout.

how_to.counts_as_done: Lights out by 11pm.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-8: most nights.

phases.title: Hold the line
phases.focus: The habits are in place — this phase is about keeping them through a stretch where the scale gets boring.

steps.title: Daily walk, 35 minutes
steps.details: Thirty-five minutes, same slot. Weekend walks can be longer and count for more than one day's worth of feeling good, but the daily bar stays thirty-five.

how_to.gist: Thirty-five minutes a day, same time as always.
how_to.why: You're in the last stretch and the walk is still the most reliable thing you do. Keeping it long keeps the scale moving when the gym gains slow down.

sections.heading: The change
sections.body: Thirty-five minutes. Same route, same slot.

sections.heading: The floor
sections.body: Twenty minutes on a bad day. Never zero.

how_to.counts_as_done: Thirty-five minutes of walking, logged.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: 35 minutes, with a longer weekend walk when you feel like it.

steps.title: Two gym sessions, still climbing
steps.details: Same two sessions and five movements. The weights should be noticeably heavier than week one by now — if they're not, that's the thing to fix this phase, not the walking.

how_to.gist: Two sessions a week, weights still going up.
how_to.why: This is what makes the difference between losing ten pounds and losing ten pounds of the wrong stuff. Keep the sessions hard right to the end.

sections.heading: The check
sections.body: Compare today's log to week one. If your main lift hasn't moved, add weight this session.

sections.heading: If you miss one
sections.body: Miss a session, do the next one. Missing two in a row is where the habit starts to go.

how_to.counts_as_done: Both sessions done.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: keep adding weight on the main lift whenever you hit the top of the rep range.

steps.title: Write down every set
steps.details: Same logbook. In the last month it's your proof that the training is still doing something even when the scale plateaus.

how_to.gist: Log every set, beat one number.
how_to.why: The scale will go flat at some point in the last month. Your log is what tells you the plan is still working when the scale says nothing.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Numbers in your phone, one number beaten per session.

sections.heading: When the scale stalls
sections.body: Open the log. If the weights are climbing, nothing is wrong — keep going and tighten the food rule instead.

how_to.counts_as_done: Both sessions logged, one number beaten.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: same standard.

steps.title: Protein at every meal
steps.details: Same 130 g. If the scale has been flat for two weeks, the fix is portion size at dinner and the extras around meals — not the protein, and not more walking.

how_to.gist: 130 g of protein, three meals, every day.
how_to.why: Holding protein steady through the last month is what keeps the loss coming off fat rather than muscle.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: About 130 g, three meals, palm-sized portions.

sections.heading: The stall response
sections.body: Two flat weeks: shrink the plate, keep the protein. Don't cut meals and don't add cardio.

how_to.counts_as_done: Three protein portions, three meals.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: same target, tighter portions if needed.

steps.title: One plate, kitchen closed after dinner
steps.details: Same rule. In the last month this is the one that decides whether you finish at ten pounds or eight.

how_to.gist: One plate at dinner, nothing afterwards.
how_to.why: The last stretch is where evening eating creeps back in. This rule is the cheapest way to protect everything you've already done.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: One plate. Kitchen closed. Water, tea or coffee only after.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: One night doesn't matter. Two in a row is the signal to move dinner later rather than snack before bed.

how_to.counts_as_done: One plate, kitchen closed.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: most nights.

steps.title: In bed by 11pm
steps.details: Same bedtime, held to the end. The last month is where people let sleep go first, and it's usually the reason the last two pounds don't come off.

how_to.gist: Lights out by 11pm.
how_to.why: Sleep is the step that quietly holds the other five together. It's also the first one to go when you get busy.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: Lights out by 11pm, seven to eight hours.

sections.heading: The run-up
sections.body: Phone across the room half an hour before bed.

how_to.counts_as_done: Lights out by 11pm.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: most nights.

milestones.title: Four weeks of walks and gym days behind you
milestones.criteria: You've walked most days and made both gym sessions in at least three of the four weeks, with the food rules running on most days.

milestones.title: The routine is automatic
milestones.criteria: Walks are 30 minutes, both gym sessions happen without deciding, and your main lift is heavier than it was in week one.

milestones.title: Ten pounds down, habits intact
milestones.criteria: You're about 10 lbs (4.5 kg) lighter than you started, still walking daily and still training twice a week — with the food rules as your default rather than a diet you're on.

protocol.coach_notes: Ten pounds in twelve weeks is a pound a week, which is the version of this that actually works — no heroics, no counting, just the walk, the two gym days, and three food rules you can check off without a calculator. The scale will be boring for stretches and then move all at once; that's normal, and the logbook is what tells you the plan is still working when the scale says nothing. One missed day is noise. The day after a miss is the one that decides this — never miss twice.

sessions.goal: I want to gain 5 lbs of lean muscle.

protocol.goal_statement: Get to bed by 11pm on weeknights for a month — lights out, phone out of the bedroom, show off by 10:30.

phases.title: Clear the chain
phases.focus: Take the phone out of the bedroom and give the show an end time — the two things that actually decide when you fall asleep.

steps.title: Phone charges in the kitchen overnight
steps.details: Every weeknight, your phone spends the night on the kitchen counter on its charger — not on the nightstand, not in the bedroom at all. Plug it in when you start winding down, and if you use it as an alarm, get a cheap alarm clock or set the 6:30 alarm on it before you walk away. This is the single biggest change in the plan: scrolling in bed is the last link in your chain, and it only works because the phone is within arm's reach.

how_to.gist: Phone on the kitchen charger before you start winding down — bedroom stays phone-free.
how_to.why: You told me the phone charges next to the bed and you scroll there. That's the last thing standing between you and sleep, and it's the one thing willpower loses to every time. Take the option away instead of fighting it.

sections.heading: The move
sections.body: When you get up off the sofa to start winding down, walk the phone to the kitchen and plug it in. It stays there until morning. If your alarm lives on the phone, set it before you walk away, or pick up a cheap alarm clock this week so there's no reason to bring it back.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: No phone in the bedroom, at all, even for 'just a minute.' One minute is how the hour starts. If you wake in the night and reach for it, it isn't there — that's the point.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: If you catch yourself scrolling in bed, don't turn it into a lost night. Walk it back to the kitchen, come back, lights out. The next night is the one that counts.

how_to.counts_as_done: Phone spent the night on the kitchen charger, not in the bedroom.

steps.week_progression: Week 1 is the whole change — hold it every weeknight from night one.

steps.title: Show off by 10:30
steps.details: The show gets a fixed end time instead of a decision at 10:45. Whatever you're watching, it stops at 10:30 — mid-episode if that's where the clock lands. Set a timer on the TV or your watch for 10:30 so the stop isn't a judgment call you have to win while you're comfortable.

how_to.gist: Timer set for 10:30; when it goes, the show goes off — mid-episode or not.
how_to.why: A show with no end time will always win the 10:45 negotiation. You named this yourself: the show runs on, then the phone in bed. Give it a stop rule so there's nothing to decide.

sections.heading: Set it up
sections.body: Before you sit down on the sofa, set a timer for 10:30 — on the TV, your watch, or the kitchen timer. The point is that something other than you calls time.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: At 10:30 the show goes off, even mid-episode. You can finish it tomorrow. Nothing you're watching is worth the hour it costs you.

sections.heading: The sofa
sections.body: When the show ends, get up. Standing up is the hard part — once you're up, the rest is easy. Straight to the bathroom, then bed.

how_to.counts_as_done: Show was off by 10:30.

steps.week_progression: Same 10:30 stop every weeknight, all four weeks.

steps.title: Lights out by 11pm
steps.details: In bed with the lights off by 11pm on weeknights. Not heading to bed at 11 — actually in it, lights out. The 10:30 show stop gives you the half hour you need to brush teeth, get ready, and be under the covers with time to spare.

how_to.gist: In bed, lights off, by 11pm on weeknights.
how_to.why: This is the goal itself. Everything else in the plan exists to make this one line easy — the phone is in the kitchen and the show is off, so 11pm is just the next thing that happens.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: Lights out at 11pm. If you're in bed at 10:55 and asleep by 11:05, that's a win. The line is the lights, not the falling asleep — you can't force sleep, only the conditions for it.

sections.heading: The runway
sections.body: Show off at 10:30 gives you thirty minutes. Teeth, face, whatever your routine is, then bed. If your routine takes longer than thirty minutes, start it earlier — the 11pm line doesn't move.

sections.heading: Weekends
sections.body: Weeknights are the target. Friday and Saturday you can stay up if you want, but try not to blow past 1am — a big weekend swing makes Monday feel like jet lag.

how_to.counts_as_done: Lights were off by 11pm.

steps.week_progression: 11pm every weeknight, weeks 1 through 4.

steps.title: Up at 6:30, alarm across the room
steps.details: Out of bed at 6:30 on weekdays, with the alarm somewhere you have to stand up to reach. Your 6:30 wake-up is the honest referee in this plan — it's what makes 11pm the only bedtime that actually works. Keep it fixed, including the morning after a late night.

how_to.gist: Up at 6:30 on weekdays, alarm out of arm's reach.
how_to.why: A fixed wake time is what pulls your bedtime earlier — sleep gets pushed from the morning end, not the night end. Your 6:30 work alarm already does this for you; the trick is not snoozing it into uselessness.

sections.heading: The setup
sections.body: Put the alarm clock (or the phone, if you use it) across the room so you have to get up to silence it. Standing up is 90% of the battle.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Out of bed at 6:30, weekdays, no matter what time you fell asleep. A late night is a reason to be tired, not a reason to sleep in — sleeping in is what pushes tomorrow's bedtime back to 1am.

sections.heading: Morning light
sections.body: Within twenty minutes of getting up, get some bright light — open the curtains, step outside, or turn on every light in the kitchen. It's the strongest thing you can do to make 11pm feel like bedtime tonight.

how_to.counts_as_done: Out of bed by 6:30 on a weekday.

steps.week_progression: 6:30 every weekday, all four weeks — this one never moves.

steps.title: Nothing new after 10:30
steps.details: After the show goes off at 10:30, you don't start anything new — no new episode, no 'quick' scroll on a laptop, no tidying the kitchen, no starting a conversation that's going to run. The half hour between 10:30 and 11 is for getting ready for bed and nothing else.

how_to.gist: After 10:30, nothing new starts — just get ready for bed.
how_to.why: The gap between 'show off' and 'in bed' is where the old pattern sneaks back in. Filling it with one more thing is how 10:30 becomes 11:30 without anyone deciding it.

sections.heading: What counts
sections.body: Starting a new episode, opening the laptop, picking up a book you can't put down, or launching into a project — all of it waits for tomorrow.

sections.heading: What's fine
sections.body: Teeth, face, pajamas, laying out tomorrow's clothes, a glass of water. Anything that moves you toward bed is fair game.

sections.heading: The test
sections.body: If you're not sure whether something counts, ask: does this end with me in bed, or does it end with me deciding when to stop? If it's the second one, it waits.

how_to.counts_as_done: Nothing new started after 10:30 — straight from show-off to bed routine.

steps.week_progression: Same rule all four weeks; by week 3 it should feel like the normal shape of the evening.

phases.title: Hold the line
phases.focus: The setup is done — now the job is not letting one late night turn into three. Same rules, tighter on the mornings after.

steps.title: Phone charges in the kitchen overnight
steps.details: Same as last week: phone on the kitchen charger every weeknight, bedroom stays phone-free. Week two is where the novelty wears off and the old habit starts making its case — 'just tonight, I need it for the alarm.' It doesn't come back in.
steps.week_progression: No change from week 1 — this is the rep that has to survive boredom.

steps.title: Show off by 10:30
steps.details: Show off at 10:30, timer and all. If the timer has started feeling optional, that's the signal to make it louder — move the timer across the room so you have to get up to silence it.
steps.week_progression: Same 10:30 stop; if you've been ignoring the timer, move it out of reach.

steps.title: Lights out by 11pm
steps.details: Lights out by 11pm on weeknights. If you missed a night last week, this is the week the plan proves it isn't fragile — one late night is noise, two in a row is how the old pattern comes back.
steps.week_progression: Same 11pm line. The goal this week is five out of five.

steps.title: Up at 6:30, alarm across the room
steps.details: Out of bed at 6:30 on weekdays, alarm across the room, bright light within twenty minutes. This is the step that keeps the whole thing honest — the morning is what makes the evening work.
steps.week_progression: Unchanged. If you've been snoozing, move the alarm further away.

steps.title: Tell one person your bedtime
steps.details: Pick one person — a partner, a friend, a coworker — and tell them you're going to bed at 11 on weeknights this month. Ask them to check in with you once a week. Saying it out loud to someone who'll ask about it is what makes a late night cost something.
steps.week_progression: One conversation this week; the weekly check-in continues through week 4.

phases.title: Make it yours
phases.focus: The rules are holding. Now build the wind-down you actually want, so the evening doesn't feel like a cage.

steps.title: Phone charges in the kitchen overnight
steps.details: Phone on the kitchen charger, every weeknight. By now this should be the thing you do without thinking about it — if it isn't yet, that's fine, keep doing it anyway.
steps.week_progression: Unchanged.

steps.title: Show off by 10:30
steps.details: Show off at 10:30. If you've found yourself not missing it much, you can swap the show for something you look forward to — a chapter of a book, a podcast, music. The point is the 10:30 stop, not the show.
steps.week_progression: Same stop time; the activity itself can change if you want it to.

steps.title: Lights out by 11pm
steps.details: Lights out by 11pm on weeknights. Three weeks in, this should be starting to feel like your normal bedtime rather than a rule you're following.
steps.week_progression: Same 11pm line, third week running.

steps.title: Up at 6:30, alarm across the room
steps.details: Out of bed at 6:30 on weekdays, bright light within twenty minutes. If you're waking before the alarm some mornings, that's the plan working — get up anyway.
steps.week_progression: Unchanged.

steps.title: Wind-down you actually like
steps.details: Pick one thing for the 10:30-to-11 half hour that you genuinely enjoy and that ends with you in bed — a chapter of a novel, a podcast with a sleep timer, stretching, tea on the couch with the lights low. The old evening had a reward built into it; this one needs one too, or the rules start feeling like punishment.
steps.week_progression: New this week — one thing you look forward to, every weeknight.

phases.title: Lock it in
phases.focus: Four weeks of 11pm. Prove it holds when the week is bad, and decide what your weekends look like.

steps.title: Phone charges in the kitchen overnight
steps.details: Phone on the kitchen charger, every weeknight. This is the habit now — the phone sleeping in the bedroom is the exception, not the default.
steps.week_progression: Unchanged. This is the one that carries the whole month.

steps.title: Show off by 10:30
steps.details: Show off at 10:30, timer set. Four weeks in, the 10:30 stop should be the thing that ends your evening, not a rule you're fighting.
steps.week_progression: Unchanged.

steps.title: Lights out by 11pm
steps.details: Lights out by 11pm on weeknights. Final week — the goal is five out of five, and the point is that it doesn't take effort anymore.
steps.week_progression: Same 11pm line; the goal this week is that it costs you nothing.

steps.title: Up at 6:30, alarm across the room
steps.details: Out of bed at 6:30 on weekdays, bright light within twenty minutes. Keep this one going after the month ends — it's what keeps the bedtime from drifting back.
steps.week_progression: Unchanged, and worth keeping permanently.

steps.title: Decide your weekend rule
steps.details: Sit down once this week and write down what your weekends look like from here — a bedtime you'll actually keep on Friday and Saturday (midnight is a reasonable one), and whether the phone still charges in the kitchen on weekend nights. A month of weeknights is easy to undo with two nights of 3am.
steps.week_progression: One decision this week that carries the habit past the four weeks.

milestones.title: Phone slept in the kitchen all five nights
milestones.criteria: Five weeknights in a row with the phone charging outside the bedroom and the show off by 10:30.

milestones.title: Five for five at 11pm
milestones.criteria: Lights out by 11pm every weeknight this week, and the 6:30 wake-up held every weekday morning.

milestones.title: The evening you built
milestones.criteria: A full week of 11pm lights-out with a wind-down you actually look forward to in the 10:30-to-11 slot.

milestones.title: A month of 11pm
milestones.criteria: Four weeks of weeknight 11pm bedtimes, phone out of the bedroom, and a weekend rule written down that keeps it going.

protocol.coach_notes: You already knew the whole chain — sofa at 10, show runs on, phone in bed — which is more than most people can say. That's why this plan doesn't ask you to want it more; it just takes the phone out of the room and puts a timer on the show, and the 11pm bedtime stops being a decision you have to win at 10:45. Week one will feel like a cage, and that's the old pattern objecting, not evidence the plan is wrong. One missed night is noise — it's the night after a miss that decides whether this sticks, so if you blow a Tuesday, Wednesday is the whole ballgame.

sessions.goal: Hold a basic 5-minute conversation in Spanish within 3 month

protocol.goal_statement: Hold a basic 5-minute conversation in Spanish in 3 months, starting from almost zero — 30 minutes each morning before work, with your Spanish-speaking partner as a live practice partner.
protocol.short_title: Hold a 5-minute Spanish conversation in 12 weeks

phases.title: Say it out loud from day one
phases.focus: Build the morning slot and start speaking real sentences to your partner immediately — no silent vocabulary phase.

steps.title: Do your 30-minute morning Spanish block
steps.details: Six mornings a week, 30 minutes before work. Ten minutes of new words and phrases, then twenty minutes saying them out loud — repeating, building your own sentences, talking to yourself in the kitchen. Sunday is your day off from this block.

how_to.gist: 30 minutes before work: 10 minutes new words, 20 minutes saying them out loud.
how_to.why: Thirty minutes a morning is the whole engine of this goal. The out-loud half is what turns words you recognize into words you can actually reach for in a conversation.

sections.heading: The block
items: 10 minutes: new words and phrases for today
20 minutes: say them out loud — repeat, then build your own sentences
Talk to yourself in the kitchen, the shower, the car

sections.heading: Where
sections.body: Same spot every morning — kitchen table, couch, wherever you already sit before work. Keep your notebook and phone there so nothing has to be fetched.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: If the morning gets eaten, do ten minutes out loud rather than skipping. Ten minutes keeps the chain; a skipped morning breaks it.

how_to.counts_as_done: 30 minutes done before work — the out-loud part is the part that counts.

steps.title: Speak Spanish with your partner for 10 minutes
steps.details: Sunday, ten minutes of real back-and-forth in Spanish. Ask her to keep it at your level and to answer in Spanish, not switch to English. Use the words you learned that week — greetings, what you did today, what you want, where things are. She corrects you after you finish a thought, not mid-sentence.

how_to.gist: Ten minutes of real Spanish back-and-forth with your partner, every Sunday.
how_to.why: She's the single biggest shortcut you have. Practising with a live person from week one means you find out what you can't say yet while there's still time to fix it.

sections.heading: How to run it
items: Ten minutes, timer on
She answers in Spanish, not English
You use this week's words — greetings, your day, what you want
Corrections come after you finish a thought, not mid-sentence

sections.heading: If you get stuck
sections.body: Say the English word and keep going. Getting stuck and working around it is the practice, not a failure of it.

sections.heading: After
sections.body: Write down the two or three things you couldn't say. Those go into Monday's block.

how_to.counts_as_done: Ten minutes of Spanish spoken with your partner on Sunday.

steps.title: Review yesterday's words before adding new ones
steps.details: First five minutes of each morning block: run through the words and phrases from the day before, out loud, before you open anything new. Words you've forgotten go back to the top of the pile. Adding new words every day without ever revisiting old ones is how people end up with a hundred words they can't use.

how_to.gist: First five minutes of the block: yesterday's words out loud, before anything new.
how_to.why: New words pile up fast and disappear just as fast. Five minutes of going back over yesterday is what makes them stay.

sections.heading: The five minutes
items: Yesterday's list, out loud, no looking first
Anything you blanked on goes to the top of today's pile
Then start the new words

sections.heading: Why it's first
sections.body: Doing it before the new material means it actually happens. Left to the end of the block, it gets dropped.

how_to.counts_as_done: Yesterday's words said out loud before you started today's new ones.

steps.title: Keep a running list of the phrases you actually need
steps.details: One page — paper or phone note — of the sentences you keep reaching for and can't say yet: ordering, asking where something is, saying you don't understand, talking about your day. Add to it whenever something comes up, and make those phrases the first thing you practise the next morning.

how_to.gist: One running list of the sentences you keep needing and can't say yet.
how_to.why: Your own gaps are better study material than any course list. Learning the sentences you actually reach for is what makes a five-minute conversation possible.

sections.heading: What goes on it
items: Sentences you wanted to say and couldn't
Things you had to say in English to your partner
Anything you had to mime or point at

sections.heading: When
sections.body: Add to it the moment it happens — during the morning block or after Sunday. Don't save it up for later.

sections.heading: Then
sections.body: The top three phrases on the list open the next morning's block.

how_to.counts_as_done: Anything you couldn't say today is written on the list.

steps.title: Put your Spanish out of sight the night before
steps.details: Before bed, set out tomorrow's material on the table where you sit — notebook open to today's page, phone on the Spanish app, nothing else on the surface. The morning version of you should be able to sit down and start without deciding anything.

how_to.gist: Set out tomorrow's Spanish material before bed so the morning needs no decisions.
how_to.why: The mornings you skip are the ones where you had to find your stuff first. Removing that step is the difference between sitting down and not.

sections.heading: Set out
items: Notebook open to today's page
Phone on the Spanish app, not the home screen
Nothing else on the table

sections.heading: Also
sections.body: Coffee cup and kettle where you'd want them. The fewer moves between waking and starting, the more mornings hold.

how_to.counts_as_done: Material is out and ready on the table before you go to bed.

steps.title: Tell your partner the plan and the Sunday slot
steps.details: Once, this week: tell your partner you're doing this for twelve weeks, that Sunday is your ten-minute Spanish slot, and ask her to hold you to it. Ask her to nudge you if a Sunday passes without it. Saying it out loud to the person you live with is what makes the Sunday slot real rather than optional.

how_to.gist: Tell your partner the twelve-week plan and ask her to hold you to the Sunday slot.
how_to.why: A plan nobody else knows about is a plan you can quietly drop. She's already part of this — making it explicit means the Sunday session happens.

sections.heading: Say this
items: I'm doing twelve weeks of Spanish, thirty minutes each morning
Sunday is our ten-minute Spanish slot
Nudge me if a Sunday goes by without it

sections.heading: One ask
sections.body: Ask her to answer you in Spanish during that slot even when it's slow going. That's the part that helps most.

how_to.counts_as_done: You've told her the plan and the Sunday slot, once.

phases.title: Hold your end up for two minutes
phases.focus: Move from single sentences to short back-and-forth exchanges, and start stretching the Sunday session past ten minutes.

steps.title: Do your 30-minute morning Spanish block
steps.details: Same six mornings, same 30 minutes — but the out-loud half now runs as short two-way exchanges with yourself: question, answer, follow-up question. Ten minutes new material, twenty minutes speaking in exchanges rather than single sentences.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-8: the out-loud half becomes question-and-answer exchanges instead of one-line repetition.

how_to.gist: Same 30 minutes, but the out-loud half is now question-answer exchanges.
how_to.why: A five-minute conversation is a chain of exchanges, not a list of sentences. Practising the chain is what gets you there.

sections.heading: The change
items: 10 minutes new words and phrases
20 minutes out loud as exchanges: ask, answer, ask again
Use the phrases from your running list

sections.heading: Example
sections.body: ¿Qué hiciste hoy? — Fui al trabajo. ¿Y tú? — Trabajé en casa. ¿Qué comiste? Keep the chain going as long as you can.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: When the chain breaks, restart it from the top rather than switching to English.

how_to.counts_as_done: 30 minutes done before work, with the out-loud half run as exchanges.

steps.title: Speak Spanish with your partner for 15 minutes
steps.details: Sunday, stretched to fifteen minutes. Pick one topic before you start — your week, a plan, something that happened — and stay in Spanish on it. She keeps answering in Spanish and corrects you after each thought.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-8: Sunday goes from 10 to 15 minutes, with a topic chosen before you start.

how_to.gist: Sunday goes to fifteen minutes on one topic, all in Spanish.
how_to.why: Staying on one topic for longer is the closest thing to the conversation you're aiming for. It's also where you find out which words you actually need.

sections.heading: Set it up
items: Pick the topic before you sit down
Fifteen minutes, timer on
Stay in Spanish the whole way
Corrections after each thought, not mid-sentence

sections.heading: If you stall
sections.body: Say the English word and keep the sentence going. Stalling and working around it is the practice.

sections.heading: After
sections.body: Two or three things you couldn't say go on the running list.

how_to.counts_as_done: Fifteen minutes of Spanish on one topic with your partner.

steps.title: Review the week's words before adding new ones
steps.details: First five minutes of the block: yesterday's words out loud, plus a quick pass over the whole week's list on Fridays. Anything you've blanked on twice goes back to the top of the pile.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-8: Friday's review covers the whole week, not just yesterday.

how_to.gist: Five minutes of yesterday's words, plus the full week's list on Friday.
how_to.why: Words you never revisit are words you can't use under pressure. The Friday pass is what keeps the earlier weeks from draining away.

sections.heading: Daily
sections.body: Yesterday's list out loud, no looking first. Anything you blanked on goes to the top of today's pile.

sections.heading: Friday
sections.body: Run the whole week's list once, out loud. Anything you've blanked on twice gets practised properly next week.

how_to.counts_as_done: Yesterday's words said out loud, and the full week's list on Friday.

steps.title: Keep a running list of the phrases you actually need
steps.details: Same list, still growing. By now it should be carrying the phrases that let you keep a conversation alive — asking someone to repeat, saying you don't understand, buying time while you think.

how_to.gist: Keep adding to the list — especially the phrases that keep a conversation alive.
how_to.why: The phrases that buy you time are what stop a conversation from collapsing when you don't catch something.

sections.heading: Add these
items: Can you repeat that?
I don't understand
How do you say…?
One moment, I'm thinking
What does that mean?

sections.heading: Then
sections.body: The top three open the next morning's block.

how_to.counts_as_done: Anything you couldn't say today is on the list.

steps.title: Put your Spanish out of sight the night before
steps.details: Same as before: notebook open, phone on the app, table clear, before bed. By week eight this should be automatic — if it isn't, that's the thing to fix, not the studying.

how_to.gist: Material out and ready before bed, same as every night.
how_to.why: This is the step that protects the mornings. When it slips, the mornings slip a few days later.

sections.heading: Set out
items: Notebook open to today's page
Phone on the Spanish app
Table clear

sections.heading: If it's slipping
sections.body: Put a note on your pillow. The point is that the morning version of you doesn't have to decide anything.

how_to.counts_as_done: Material is out and ready before you go to bed.

phases.title: Stretch it to five minutes
phases.focus: Push the Sunday session to the full five minutes and beyond, and start using Spanish in small real-world moments.

steps.title: Do your 30-minute morning Spanish block
steps.details: Same six mornings, same 30 minutes. The out-loud half is now full mock conversations: pick a situation — a shop, a neighbour, a phone call — and run it start to finish out loud, twice, fixing what broke the first time.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: the out-loud half becomes full mock conversations run start to finish.

how_to.gist: 30 minutes, with the out-loud half run as full mock conversations.
how_to.why: Running a whole situation start to finish is the last step before doing it with a real person. It's where the pieces stop being separate.

sections.heading: The change
items: 10 minutes new words and phrases
20 minutes running one situation out loud, start to finish
Run it twice — fix what broke the first time

sections.heading: Situations to use
items: Buying something in a shop
Talking to a neighbour about the weather
Ordering food
A phone call to book something
Explaining what you did at the weekend

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: No stopping to look things up mid-run. Finish the situation, then look up what you fumbled.

how_to.counts_as_done: 30 minutes done before work, with one full situation run out loud.

steps.title: Speak Spanish with your partner for 5 minutes straight
steps.details: Sunday: five minutes of unbroken Spanish with your partner, no English, no switching. Timer on, one topic or a natural drift between topics. This is the thing you set out to do — do it every Sunday from here, and if it goes past five minutes, let it.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: Sunday becomes the full five minutes unbroken — the target itself.

how_to.gist: Five minutes of unbroken Spanish with your partner, no English.
how_to.why: This is the goal, rehearsed weekly. Doing it four Sundays running is what makes it something you can do on demand rather than on a good day.

sections.heading: How
items: Timer on for five minutes
No English, no switching
One topic, or let it drift naturally
If it goes past five minutes, keep going

sections.heading: If you get stuck
sections.body: Use the phrases that buy you time — 'one moment', 'can you repeat that'. Getting through a stall in Spanish is the whole skill.

sections.heading: After
sections.body: Two or three things you couldn't say go on the running list for Monday.

how_to.counts_as_done: Five minutes of unbroken Spanish with your partner, timer on.

steps.title: Use Spanish in one real moment outside the house
steps.details: Twice a week, use Spanish with someone who isn't your partner: greet the person at the counter, order in Spanish, say thank you and goodbye in Spanish, ask a shop worker where something is. Short is fine. The point is doing it with a stranger who won't fill in your gaps for you.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: new — real-world Spanish with people other than your partner.

how_to.gist: Twice a week, say something in Spanish to someone who isn't your partner.
how_to.why: Your partner knows what you're trying to say. A stranger doesn't — and that's the situation the five-minute conversation actually happens in.

sections.heading: Easy ones
items: Greet the person at the counter
Order your coffee in Spanish
Ask where something is in a shop
Say thank you and goodbye in Spanish

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Short counts. One sentence to a stranger is a rep. Don't wait until you can do more.

sections.heading: If they answer in English
sections.body: That's fine — you still said it. Say it again next time.

how_to.counts_as_done: Two separate moments this week where you spoke Spanish to someone other than your partner.

steps.title: Review the week's words before adding new ones
steps.details: First five minutes: yesterday's words out loud, and the full week's list on Friday. By now the Friday pass should be quick — the words that stuck need one pass, the ones that didn't need three.

how_to.gist: Five minutes of yesterday's words, full week's list on Friday.
how_to.why: Twelve weeks of new words only stays useful if you keep going back over it. This is the cheapest five minutes in the plan.

sections.heading: Daily
sections.body: Yesterday's list out loud, no looking first.

sections.heading: Friday
sections.body: The whole week's list, out loud. Anything you've blanked on twice gets drilled properly next week.

how_to.counts_as_done: Yesterday's words said out loud, and the full week's list on Friday.

steps.title: Put your Spanish out of sight the night before
steps.details: Same nightly setup: notebook open, phone on the app, table clear. Twelve weeks in, this is the habit that carried the other ones.

how_to.gist: Material out and ready before bed — the nightly setup that protects the mornings.
how_to.why: Every morning you've done started the night before. Keep it going to the end.

sections.heading: Set out
items: Notebook open to today's page
Phone on the Spanish app
Table clear

sections.heading: Keep it
sections.body: Don't retire this one at the finish line. It's what makes the mornings happen without a decision.

how_to.counts_as_done: Material is out and ready before you go to bed.

milestones.title: Four weeks of mornings, unbroken
milestones.criteria: You've done the 30-minute morning block on at least 20 of the 24 scheduled mornings, and had four Sunday Spanish sessions with your partner.

milestones.title: Fifteen minutes on one topic
milestones.criteria: You've held a fifteen-minute Spanish conversation with your partner on a single topic, and your running list has grown past fifty phrases.

milestones.title: Five minutes, no English
milestones.criteria: You've held five minutes of unbroken Spanish with your partner, and used Spanish with a stranger at least eight times over the last four weeks.

protocol.coach_notes: Weeks two through four are the ones to watch: starting from twenty words means the progress is real but invisible, and that flat stretch is where most Spanish attempts quietly stop. The mornings are the whole engine here — one missed morning is noise, but two in a row is how the slot dies, so the morning after a miss is the one that matters. You already have the two things most learners are missing: a fixed time and a person who speaks the language. Use her as a sparring partner from week one, not a dictionary.

sessions.goal: Walk 10,000 steps a day consistently. I currently average ab

protocol.goal_statement: Build from ~4,000 to a consistent 10,000 steps a day, anchored to a 20-30 minute lunch walk plus an after-work walk.
protocol.short_title: Walk 10,000 steps a day in 10 weeks

phases.title: Hold the two slots
phases.focus: The number doesn't matter yet — the two walks happening every workday is the whole job. Get out at lunch, get out after work, and let the steps land where they land.

steps.title: Lunch walk
steps.details: Out the door at lunch for 20 minutes of walking. Same time each day, before you eat or right after — pick one and keep it. Busy day? 15 minutes still counts as done.

how_to.gist: Walk 20 minutes at lunch, every workday, rain or shine.
how_to.why: This is the walk that carries the whole goal. Your days are mostly sitting, so lunch is the one slot where the day is still yours — and it's the walk most likely to get cancelled when work runs hot, which is exactly why it gets a floor instead of a target.

sections.heading: The week
sections.body: Monday through Friday, 20 minutes. Put it in your calendar as a real appointment at the same time each day — the same time is what makes it happen without deciding.

sections.heading: The floor
sections.body: On a day that blows up, 15 minutes still counts. A short walk you take beats a long walk you skip, and the streak stays alive either way.

sections.heading: Where to go
sections.body: Any loop that gets you out of the building. If you can, pick a route with a bit of green or a stretch away from traffic — you'll take it more often.

how_to.counts_as_done: 20 minutes of walking outside the office at lunch (15 on a bad day).

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 20 minutes, five workdays. The time stays fixed — only your habit of showing up is being built.

steps.title: After-work walk
steps.details: 15 minutes on your feet after work — before you sit down at home, not after. Shoes by the door, walk out the front door, come back. Short on purpose.

how_to.gist: 15 minutes on your feet right after work, before you sit down.
how_to.why: The lunch walk alone won't get you to 10,000. This one is deliberately short so it survives tired evenings — a 15-minute walk you actually take beats a 45-minute one you talk yourself out of.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Walk before you sit down. Once you're on the couch, this walk is gone — so shoes off at the door, straight back out.

sections.heading: Set it up
sections.body: Leave your walking shoes by the front door in the morning. Coming home to shoes already waiting removes the one decision that kills this walk.

sections.heading: If you're wiped
sections.body: Go anyway, even a slow loop around the block. Tired legs still count; a skipped walk doesn't.

how_to.counts_as_done: 15 minutes of walking after work, before sitting down.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 15 minutes, five workdays. Length grows later — right now it just needs to happen.

steps.title: Saturday long walk
steps.details: One longer walk on Saturday — 40 minutes, somewhere you actually like going. This is the day you bank extra steps without it feeling like exercise.

how_to.gist: One 40-minute walk on Saturday, somewhere you enjoy.
how_to.why: Weekdays are capped by your calendar. Saturday is the one day you can walk longer without squeezing it in — it lifts your weekly total and gives your legs a longer, easier effort than the short weekday loops.

sections.heading: Where
sections.body: Pick a place worth going to: a park, a waterfront, a neighbourhood you like. Enjoying the route is what makes this the easy day instead of the chore day.

sections.heading: Pace
sections.body: Easy and conversational. You should be able to talk the whole way — this is about time on your feet, not speed.

how_to.counts_as_done: 40 minutes of walking on Saturday.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 40 minutes. Grows to 50 in phase 2 and 60 in phase 3.

steps.title: Daily step count
steps.details: Hit at least 5,000 steps today. That's barely above where you already are — the point is to see the number every day and watch it climb, not to chase it yet.

how_to.gist: At least 5,000 steps today — just above your current average.
how_to.why: You're at about 4,000 now. Asking for 10,000 in week one is how step goals die. Starting at 5,000 means the two walks alone get you there, and the target climbs about 600 a week from here.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: 5,000 steps minimum, every day including weekends. Check your phone or watch whenever suits you — once in the evening is plenty.

sections.heading: Why so low
sections.body: The walks are the real work in these first weeks. The number is here so you can see the trend, not so you can pass or fail a day.

sections.heading: If you're short
sections.body: A 10-minute loop after dinner closes most gaps. Don't save it for tomorrow.

how_to.counts_as_done: Your step count for the day reads 5,000 or more.

steps.week_progression: 5,000 in week 1, 5,600 in week 2, 6,200 in week 3 — roughly 600 more each week.

steps.title: Shoes and route ready the night before
steps.details: Before bed, put your walking shoes by the front door and know where tomorrow's lunch walk goes. Two minutes of setup that decides whether the walks happen.

how_to.gist: Shoes by the door and tomorrow's route decided, before bed.
how_to.why: Both walks die at the same moment: the second you have to decide and hunt for gear. Doing it the night before means tomorrow you just put the shoes on and go.

sections.heading: The setup
items: Walking shoes by the front door
Tomorrow's lunch walk route decided (same loop is fine)
Work bag packed so lunch is free

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The lunch walk is the one that gets cancelled when work runs hot. Having everything ready removes the easiest excuse for cancelling it.

how_to.counts_as_done: Shoes by the door and tomorrow's route decided before you go to bed.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: every worknight. Once it's automatic you can drop it from the list.

phases.title: Climb the number
phases.focus: The two walks are running — now the step target climbs underneath them, and the walks get a little longer to carry it.

steps.title: Lunch walk
steps.details: 25 minutes at lunch, five workdays. Same slot as before, five minutes longer. 15 minutes still counts on a day that goes sideways.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-7: 25 minutes. The slot is fixed; only the length moves.

steps.title: After-work walk
steps.details: 20 minutes after work, before you sit down. Still short enough to survive a tired evening.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-7: 20 minutes, five workdays.

steps.title: Saturday long walk
steps.details: 50 minutes on Saturday, easy pace, somewhere you like. This is the day that makes the weekly total comfortable.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-7: 50 minutes.

steps.title: Daily step count
steps.details: At least 7,500 steps today. The longer walks should carry you there without extra effort — if you're short, a short evening loop closes the gap.
steps.week_progression: 6,800 in week 4, 7,500 in week 5, 8,200 in week 6, 8,800 in week 7.

steps.title: Take the stairs and stand every hour
steps.details: Stairs instead of the lift, and get up out of the chair once an hour at work. Small steps that add up across a desk day without adding a walk.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-7: every workday. These are the steps that fill the gap on days the walks run short.

phases.title: Land on 10,000
phases.focus: The target reaches 10,000 and stays there. The walks hold the floor; the rest of the day fills in around them.

steps.title: Lunch walk
steps.details: 30 minutes at lunch, five workdays. This is the full length you said you could do — hold it here.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: 30 minutes, five workdays.

steps.title: After-work walk
steps.details: 25 minutes after work, before you sit down. Between this and lunch you're already most of the way to 10,000 before dinner.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: 25 minutes, five workdays.

steps.title: Saturday long walk
steps.details: 60 minutes on Saturday, easy pace. An hour on your feet, somewhere worth going.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: 60 minutes.

steps.title: Daily step count
steps.details: 10,000 steps today. The two walks plus a normal day should land you here — the last stretch is usually a short loop after dinner.
steps.week_progression: 9,400 in week 8, 10,000 in weeks 9 and 10. Hold it, don't chase more.

steps.title: Sunday walk
steps.details: 40 minutes on Sunday. Weekends are where step counts quietly collapse — this keeps Sunday from undoing the week.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: 40 minutes every Sunday.

steps.title: Take the stairs and stand every hour
steps.details: Stairs instead of the lift, up out of the chair once an hour. Keep this running — it's what makes 10,000 hold on busy days.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 8-10: every workday.

milestones.title: Two full weeks of both walks
milestones.criteria: Both the lunch walk and the after-work walk happened on every workday for two straight weeks, and your daily count has been sitting above 5,000.

milestones.title: Averaging over 7,000 a day
milestones.criteria: Your weekly average is above 7,000 steps a day and the Saturday walk is a normal part of your week.

milestones.title: Ten thousand, held
milestones.criteria: You've averaged 10,000 steps a day across the final two weeks, with the lunch walk and the after-work walk both still happening.

protocol.coach_notes: You already did the hard part before we started: you named when the walking happens. Most people never get that far, which is why most step goals quietly die by week three. The plan just ladders the number up underneath the two slots you picked — about 600 steps a week, which is slow enough to feel like nothing. The lunch walk is the one that matters most; on a day when work runs hot, take the 15-minute version rather than skipping it, because the walk after a missed day is the one that decides whether this sticks. One missed day is noise. Two in a row is how habits end.
