protocol.goal_statement: Run a continuous 4k — no walking breaks — in 10 weeks, starting from brisk walking with three morning runs a week.

phases.title: Get the mornings running
phases.focus: Three mornings a week, every week. Short run-walk blocks you can finish easily — the point of these weeks is showing up, not speed.

steps.title: Morning run-walk session
steps.details: Out the door Monday, Wednesday and Friday before work. Warm up with 5 minutes of brisk walking, then alternate 1 minute of easy jogging with 2 minutes of walking for 15 minutes, then walk the last 5 minutes home. Jog at a pace where you could still talk in short sentences.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3 keep the same 1 minute on / 2 minutes off shape. If a jog block feels hard, slow the jog down rather than cutting it short.

how_to.gist: 25 minutes: 5 min walk, then 1 min jog / 2 min walk x5, then 5 min walk home.
how_to.why: You can already walk briskly for a long stretch — this takes that base and adds short running blocks small enough that your legs and breathing can absorb them. It's the first rung of getting to a continuous 4k.

sections.heading: The week
items: Monday — run-walk session
Tuesday — rest
Wednesday — run-walk session
Thursday — rest
Friday — run-walk session
Saturday and Sunday — rest

sections.heading: The session
items: 5 minutes brisk walk to warm up
1 minute easy jog, then 2 minutes walking — repeat 5 times
5 minutes walking to finish

sections.heading: The pace
sections.body: The jog blocks should feel almost too easy. If you're gasping, you're going too fast — slow down until you could say a short sentence out loud while jogging. Finishing all five blocks matters far more than how quick they are.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: If you miss a morning, do the next one as planned — don't try to make it up by doubling up. Two missed mornings in a row is the signal to reset: same session, next scheduled day, no punishment.

how_to.counts_as_done: All 5 jog blocks completed in one outing, 3 outings this week.

steps.title: Lay the kit out the night before
steps.details: The night before each run morning, put your trainers, socks and running clothes by the door or on the chair you'll walk past. Fill a water bottle and leave it with them. Nothing to find, nothing to decide at 6am.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: every run morning gets a laid-out kit. Keep it going even once it feels automatic — it's the cheapest thing in the plan.

how_to.gist: Night before each run morning: trainers, socks, clothes and water by the door.
how_to.why: The hardest part of a 6am run is the five minutes before you leave the house. Removing every small decision and search makes leaving the default instead of a choice.

sections.heading: What to set out
items: Trainers and socks
The clothes you'll run in
Filled water bottle
Anything you take with you — keys, phone, headphones

sections.heading: Where
sections.body: By the front door, or on a chair you walk past on the way out. Visible, not in a drawer. If you'd have to open a cupboard to find it, it isn't set out.

sections.heading: When
sections.body: Before you go to bed on Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday nights — those are the nights before your three run mornings.

how_to.counts_as_done: Kit was out and waiting before bed, on all three nights before a run morning.

steps.title: Walk 20 minutes on the off days
steps.details: On the two mornings between your runs, walk briskly for 20 minutes. Same park, same route, no jogging. This keeps the habit of going out on a run-week morning without adding running load to legs that are still adapting.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 20 brisk minutes. If your legs feel heavy from the run days, walk slower — the point is the outing, not the pace.

how_to.gist: 20 brisk minutes of walking on Tuesday and Thursday mornings.
how_to.why: Three run days in a row would be too much for legs that have never run. Walking on the days between keeps the morning routine intact and builds the base your running sits on.

sections.heading: The walk
sections.body: 20 minutes at a pace that's purposeful but comfortable — faster than a stroll, slower than a march. Same park and route as your run mornings so the whole week feels like one routine.

sections.heading: Why not run
sections.body: Your legs need the days between runs to recover. Walking gives you the morning out without the pounding, and it's the reason you'll still be running in week eight.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: If a walk morning gets eaten, let it go and take the next run morning as planned. Don't swap it for an extra run.

how_to.counts_as_done: Two 20-minute walks done this week.

phases.title: Shrink the walking
phases.focus: The jog blocks get longer and the walk breaks get shorter. Same three mornings, same route — the shape of the session is what changes.

steps.title: Morning run-walk session
steps.details: Monday, Wednesday and Friday before work. 5 minutes brisk walking to warm up, then alternate 3 minutes of easy jogging with 2 minutes of walking for 20 minutes, then walk 5 minutes to finish. Keep the jog conversational.
steps.week_progression: Week 4: 3 min jog / 2 min walk. Week 5: 4 min jog / 2 min walk. Week 6: 5 min jog / 2 min walk. Same total time each week — the jog blocks just get longer.

how_to.gist: 30 minutes: 5 min walk, then 3 min jog / 2 min walk x4, then 5 min walk home.
how_to.why: Your legs now know what jogging feels like. Stretching the jog blocks and trimming the walking is how the walking breaks eventually disappear — this is the middle of the road to a continuous 4k.

sections.heading: The session
items: 5 minutes brisk walk
3 minutes easy jog, then 2 minutes walking — repeat 4 times
5 minutes walking to finish

sections.heading: Each week
items: Week 4 — 3 min jog / 2 min walk
Week 5 — 4 min jog / 2 min walk
Week 6 — 5 min jog / 2 min walk

sections.heading: The pace
sections.body: As the jog blocks get longer, the temptation is to speed up. Don't. Hold the same easy, talkable pace you used in weeks 1-3 — the extra time is the training, not the speed.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: If a week feels too hard, repeat that week's shape before moving on. Repeating a week costs you nothing; pushing through a week you weren't ready for costs you a run morning.

how_to.counts_as_done: All jog blocks in the session completed, 3 sessions this week.

steps.title: Lay the kit out the night before
steps.details: Same as before: trainers, socks, clothes and water by the door the night before each run morning. By now it should be a two-minute job — keep doing it anyway.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-6: unchanged. This is the habit that makes the other ones possible.

steps.title: Walk 25 minutes on the off days
steps.details: Tuesday and Thursday mornings, 25 brisk minutes in the park. No jogging. This is your recovery day and your base-building day at once.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-6: 25 minutes, up from 20. Keep it comfortable.

steps.title: Note how the jog blocks felt
steps.details: Right after each run morning, take ten seconds to note one thing: which jog block felt hardest, or whether the last one felt easier than the first. One line, on your phone or in your head on the walk home. It's how you'll know whether to repeat a week or move on.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-6: after every run morning. If two weeks in a row feel rough, repeat the shape before progressing.

phases.title: Close the gaps
phases.focus: The walking breaks get short and then disappear. By the end of this phase you're running the whole thing, just not yet at 4k.

steps.title: Morning run session
steps.details: Monday, Wednesday and Friday before work. 5 minutes brisk walking to warm up, then run continuously for 20 minutes at an easy, talkable pace, then walk 5 minutes to cool down. If you truly need a break, take one 1-minute walk in the middle — but aim for none.
steps.week_progression: Week 7: 20 minutes continuous. Week 8: 25 minutes continuous. Same easy pace throughout — the distance grows because the time grows.

how_to.gist: 32 minutes: 5 min walk, 20 min continuous easy run, 5 min walk home.
how_to.why: This is the week the walking breaks go away. Twenty minutes of continuous running is the last big step before the full 4k — and it's shorter than you think.

sections.heading: The session
items: 5 minutes brisk walk to warm up
20 minutes continuous easy running
5 minutes walking to cool down

sections.heading: The pace
sections.body: Slower than feels natural. The whole point of this phase is covering the time without stopping — speed comes later, or not at all. If you're breathing hard enough that you can't speak a sentence, ease off.

sections.heading: If you need a break
sections.body: One 1-minute walk in the middle is allowed if you genuinely need it. Note it, finish the session, and repeat the week rather than moving on. A break you planned for is not a failure; a break you didn't expect is information.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: Missed a morning? Take the next one as scheduled. Never run two days in a row to catch up — the rest days are doing work.

how_to.counts_as_done: 20 minutes (week 7) or 25 minutes (week 8) of continuous running, 3 sessions this week.

steps.title: Lay the kit out the night before
steps.details: Trainers, socks, clothes and water by the door the night before each run morning. Unchanged.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 7-8: unchanged.

steps.title: Walk 25 minutes on the off days
steps.details: Tuesday and Thursday mornings, 25 brisk minutes. These days are now genuinely recovery — your run days are doing real work, so keep these easy.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 7-8: unchanged at 25 minutes.

steps.title: Note how the run felt
steps.details: After each run morning, note whether you got through the continuous block without stopping, and roughly how far you covered. Two lines. This is how you'll know you're ready for the 4k.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 7-8: after every run morning.

phases.title: The 4k
phases.focus: Extend the continuous run to 4k, then do it for real. The last two weeks are about distance, not speed.

steps.title: Morning run session
steps.details: Monday, Wednesday and Friday before work. 5 minutes brisk walking to warm up, then run continuously for 30 minutes (week 9) or the full 4k (week 10) at an easy pace, then walk 5 minutes to cool down.
steps.week_progression: Week 9: 30 minutes continuous — for most people that's already close to 4k. Week 10: the full 4k, no walking breaks, on all three mornings.

how_to.gist: 5 min walk, then 30 min continuous run (week 9) or the full 4k (week 10), then 5 min walk.
how_to.why: This is the goal itself. Everything before this was building the legs and lungs to run 4k without stopping — now you just do it.

sections.heading: Week 9
sections.body: Run 30 continuous minutes at your easy pace. Don't chase the distance — if 30 minutes gets you past 4k, great; if it doesn't, you're close and week 10 will finish the job.

sections.heading: Week 10
sections.body: Run the full 4k, all three mornings, no walking breaks. Same easy pace as every other week. Pick a flat route in the park you already know so the only variable is you.

sections.heading: The pace
sections.body: Start slower than you want to. The most common way to miss a 4k is to go out too fast in the first kilometre. If you can speak a sentence at the halfway point, you're pacing it right.

sections.heading: If it doesn't happen
sections.body: If week 10's 4k doesn't come off on the first try, repeat the week. You're not starting over — you're finishing. Take the next scheduled morning and go again.

how_to.counts_as_done: Week 9: 30 continuous minutes, 3 sessions. Week 10: a full 4k with no walking breaks, 3 sessions.

steps.title: Lay the kit out the night before
steps.details: Trainers, socks, clothes and water by the door the night before each run morning. Unchanged — this is the habit that got you here.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-10: unchanged.

steps.title: Walk 20 minutes on the off days
steps.details: Tuesday and Thursday mornings, 20 easy minutes. Trimmed back from 25 so your legs are fresh for the longer run days.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-10: 20 minutes, easy. Fresh legs matter more than extra walking now.

steps.title: Note the distance covered
steps.details: After each run morning, note how far you went. Week 9 tells you how close you are; week 10 tells you it's done. The first number you log is your starting point — no need to guess one now.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-10: after every run morning. Watch the number climb toward 4.

milestones.title: Three weeks of mornings, held
milestones.criteria: You've done all three run-walk mornings and both walk mornings for three weeks running. The routine exists now — that was the part most plans never get to.

milestones.title: Jogging 5 minutes at a stretch
milestones.criteria: Your run-walk blocks are up to 5 minutes of continuous jogging, three mornings a week. Week six was the original deadline — you've now got the base that deadline was missing.

milestones.title: 25 minutes, no walking
milestones.criteria: You ran 25 continuous minutes without a walking break, three mornings in a row. The walking breaks are gone — only the distance is left.

milestones.title: A continuous 4k
milestones.criteria: You ran 4k without stopping, and you did it on all three mornings of the week. That's the goal, done.

protocol.coach_notes: Ten weeks instead of six isn't a smaller goal — it's the same goal with enough runway to actually land. The three mornings you already have are the hard part, and they don't change once in this whole plan. One missed morning is noise; the morning after a miss is the one that decides whether this sticks, so never let two go by in a row. See you at 4k.

sessions.goal: Learn to bake a proper layered birthday cake from scratch in

protocol.goal_statement: Bake a proper layered birthday cake from scratch — sponge, filling, frosting, stacked and finished — within a month, on one long weekend session plus one weeknight per week.
protocol.short_title: Bake a layered birthday cake in 4 weeks

phases.title: Learn the sponge
phases.focus: Get one plain sponge right, twice, and set up your kitchen so the weekend bake starts without hunting for anything.

steps.title: Bake a plain two-layer sponge
steps.details: One long weekend session. Weigh everything out before you start, line two tins with baking paper, and bake a basic Victoria-style sponge — equal weights of butter, sugar, flour and eggs, whisked by hand until pale and thick. Let the layers cool completely in the tins. You are not decorating anything today; today is only about a sponge that rises evenly and comes out of the tin in one piece.

how_to.gist: Bake one plain two-layer sponge, start to finish, and let it cool in the tins.
how_to.why: Every other skill in this plan sits on top of a sponge that works. Get this one right and frosting and stacking become easy; skip it and you're decorating a crumbly mess.

sections.heading: Before you start
items: Weigh all four ingredients out into separate bowls first — no mid-bake measuring
Line the bottom of both tins with baking paper and grease the sides
Oven on at 180°C / 350°F to heat while you mix

sections.heading: The mix
sections.body: Beat the soft butter and sugar with your hand whisk until it's pale and noticeably lighter — this takes longer by hand than a recipe suggests, so give it a full 4-5 minutes. Add the eggs one at a time, whisking each in fully. Fold the flour in with a spoon in three goes, stopping the moment it's combined. Divide between the two tins and smooth the tops.

sections.heading: The bake
sections.body: Bake until the tops spring back when you press them lightly and a skewer comes out clean — start checking at 22 minutes. Cool in the tins for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a rack and leave them completely cold before you touch them again.

sections.heading: If it goes wrong
sections.body: A sunken middle usually means the oven door was opened early or the mix was under-beaten. A dry sponge means it baked too long. Either way, write down what happened and bake it again next weekend — a failed sponge is information, not a setback.

how_to.counts_as_done: Two sponge layers baked, cooled and turned out of the tins in one piece.

steps.week_progression: Week 1: follow the recipe exactly, no changes. Week 2 onward: same recipe, but you're aiming to beat your own mixing time and get a more even rise.

steps.title: Set up your baking shelf
steps.details: One-time job, do it before your first bake. Clear one shelf or one box and put everything the cake needs in it: tins, baking paper, whisk, scales, spatula, cooling rack. Next to it, write your recipe on a single card and stick it to the cupboard door. The point is that on bake day you open one door and everything is there — no digging, no missing scales halfway through.

how_to.gist: Clear one shelf and put every cake tool and ingredient on it, recipe card included.
how_to.why: The most common way a bake dies is a ten-minute hunt for the scales while the butter softens. One shelf means the session starts the moment you decide to start.

sections.heading: What goes on it
items: Two tins and the baking paper
Hand whisk, spatula, scales
Cooling rack
Your recipe, written on one card and taped inside the cupboard door

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Nothing else lives on this shelf. If you cook something else and the whisk ends up in the sink, it goes back on the shelf when it's washed. The shelf stays the cake shelf.

how_to.counts_as_done: One shelf or box holds every cake tool, and the recipe card is up.

steps.week_progression: One-time setup in week 1; from then on it's just keeping the shelf intact.

steps.title: Read the recipe through and shop for Saturday
steps.details: Your weeknight slot. Read Saturday's recipe end to end once, out loud if it helps, then check what you're short of and buy it. Butter out of the fridge the night before so it's soft by Saturday morning. This is a 20-minute job and it is the difference between a bake that starts at 9am and one that starts at 11 after a shop.

how_to.gist: Read Saturday's recipe once, buy what's missing, and put the butter out to soften.
how_to.why: Baking punishes improvisation. Twenty minutes on Wednesday buys you a Saturday that starts on time with soft butter and everything in the house.

sections.heading: The weeknight job
items: Read the whole recipe once, start to finish
Check the shelf against the ingredient list
Buy anything missing
Butter out of the fridge onto the counter

sections.heading: Why the butter matters
sections.body: Cold butter won't cream, and creaming by hand is already the slow part. Butter that's been out overnight is the single easiest thing you can do to make Saturday's mixing easier on your arm.

how_to.counts_as_done: Recipe read, ingredients in the house, butter out of the fridge.

steps.week_progression: Same job every week — the recipe changes, the routine doesn't.

steps.title: Write down what happened after each bake
steps.details: Two minutes at the end of every bake, before you clean up. On the back of your recipe card note the date, how long you mixed, how long it baked, and one thing you'd change next time. Next week you read that note before you start. Four bakes without notes is four first bakes.

how_to.gist: Two minutes after each bake: date, mix time, bake time, one change for next time.
how_to.why: You're a beginner doing four bakes, not forty. The only way four bakes teach you anything is if you write down what the last one told you.

sections.heading: What to write
items: Date
How long you mixed (roughly)
How long it baked
One thing you'd change

sections.heading: When
sections.body: Do it while the cake is cooling and the kitchen still smells of it — not later that evening, when the details have gone.

how_to.counts_as_done: This week's bake is noted on the recipe card.

steps.week_progression: Every week. By week 4 the card is your own recipe, not the book's.

phases.title: Frosting and filling
phases.focus: Learn to make a frosting that holds up by hand, and a filling that tastes like something — on their own, before they ever meet a cake.

steps.title: Bake the sponge again, this time to split into three
steps.details: Same sponge recipe as last week, but bake it as three thin layers (or two, then slice one horizontally once cold). You're practising the same mix with a new shape, and you'll have layers ready for next week's assembly. Cool fully, then wrap and freeze them if you're not using them within a day.

how_to.gist: Bake the same sponge as three thin layers, cool, wrap and freeze.
how_to.why: A three-layer cake is the thing you're actually aiming at, and thin layers bake faster and level more easily. Doing it now means next week is assembly, not baking.

sections.heading: The change from last week
sections.body: Same ingredients, same method, divided across three tins instead of two. Thinner layers bake quicker — start checking at 15 minutes and trust the skewer, not the clock.

sections.heading: Splitting a layer
sections.body: If you only have two tins, bake two layers, cool them completely, then run a long serrated knife around the middle of one, keeping the blade level, and ease it through. Cold cake slices cleanly; warm cake tears.

sections.heading: Storing them
sections.body: Cool completely, then wrap each layer tightly in cling film and freeze. Frozen layers are actually easier to frost — less crumb, less sliding.

how_to.counts_as_done: Three sponge layers baked, cooled and wrapped.

steps.week_progression: Week 2 only — this is the layer stock for the rest of the plan.

steps.title: Make a hand-whisked buttercream
steps.details: Your second bake of the weekend, and the one that matters most. Soft butter, icing sugar, a splash of milk or vanilla, whisked by hand until it's smooth, thick and holds a peak. Do it on its own — no cake involved — so you can see what it looks like when it's right and what it looks like when it splits. If it goes grainy or soupy, warm the bowl slightly and keep going; it comes back.

how_to.gist: Whisk a bowl of buttercream by hand until it's smooth and holds a peak.
how_to.why: Frosting is the hard part without a stand mixer, and it's the part that makes a cake look bought rather than homemade. Learning it on its own means you're not learning it at the end of a long bake with a tired arm.

sections.heading: The mix
items: Butter genuinely soft — press it, it should give easily
Icing sugar added in three or four goes, not all at once
A tablespoon of milk or vanilla to loosen it
Whisk steadily; expect 5-8 minutes by hand

sections.heading: What right looks like
sections.body: Smooth, thick, holds a soft peak on the whisk, and doesn't slide off a spoon held upside down. If it looks curdled, it's usually temperature — put the bowl somewhere warm for five minutes and keep whisking.

sections.heading: If it splits
sections.body: Grainy or separated buttercream is nearly always cold butter or cold room. Warm the bowl in a sink of warm water for a minute, then whisk again. Don't throw it out — it comes back almost every time.

how_to.counts_as_done: A bowl of buttercream that's smooth and holds a peak.

steps.week_progression: Week 2: get it smooth. Week 3 and 4: same method, but you're aiming for it to take less time and less arm.

steps.title: Make a fruit filling and taste it against the frosting
steps.details: Cook down berries or jam with a squeeze of lemon until it's thick enough to hold its shape on a cold spoon, then cool it completely. Spread a spoon of it next to a spoon of your buttercream and taste both together. You're checking the balance now, on spoons, rather than finding out it's too sweet when it's already inside the cake.

how_to.gist: Cook a thick fruit filling, cool it, and taste it with the buttercream.
how_to.why: A layered cake is sponge, filling and frosting in every bite. If the filling is thin it soaks the sponge and the cake slides; if it's too sweet the whole thing tastes flat.

sections.heading: Getting it thick
sections.body: Simmer the fruit with a squeeze of lemon, stirring, until a spoon dragged through leaves a clear trail and a drop on a cold plate doesn't run. That's 10-15 minutes for most berries. Cool it completely — warm filling melts frosting.

sections.heading: The taste test
sections.body: One spoon of filling, one of buttercream, together. Too sweet? More lemon in the filling. Too sharp? A little more sugar. Adjust now, while it's still in bowls.

how_to.counts_as_done: Filling cooked, cooled, and tasted alongside the frosting.

steps.week_progression: Week 2 only — from week 3 the filling goes into the cake.

steps.title: Read next week's assembly plan and shop for it
steps.details: Weeknight slot. Read through how you'll stack and frost the cake next Saturday, then buy anything missing — a cake board or plate, a turntable or a lazy Susan if you have one, a palette knife or a plain butter knife, and a piping bag or a freezer bag with the corner cut off. Butter out for the weekend.

how_to.gist: Read the stacking plan, buy the board and tools, put the butter out.
how_to.why: Stacking day needs a board, something to spread with, and a plan. Buying them on Wednesday means Saturday is assembly, not a trip to the shop with frosting already made.

sections.heading: What you need
items: A cake board or a flat plate you don't mind frosting on
A palette knife, or a plain table knife
A piping bag, or a freezer bag with a corner snipped
A turntable or lazy Susan if you have one — not essential
Butter out of the fridge

sections.heading: Read the plan
sections.body: Know the order before Saturday: trim the layers level, filling between each, a thin coat all over, chill, then the final coat. Reading it once now means you're not reading it with sticky hands.

how_to.counts_as_done: Assembly plan read, board and tools in the house, butter out.

steps.week_progression: Same weeknight routine each week; only the list changes.

phases.title: Stack and frost
phases.focus: Build the actual cake — layers level, filling between them, a crumb coat, then a clean finish.

steps.title: Stack and fill the cake
steps.details: Long weekend session. Trim the tops of your layers flat with a serrated knife, put the first layer on the board, pipe a ring of buttercream around the edge, spoon filling inside the ring, then the next layer. Repeat. The buttercream ring is the dam that stops the filling squeezing out the sides when you press down — press gently, and check the stack is level with your eye before you move on.

how_to.gist: Trim the layers flat, then stack them with a buttercream ring and filling between each.
how_to.why: This is the moment it stops being sponges and becomes a cake. A level stack with a dam around the filling is what keeps it from sliding apart on the plate.

sections.heading: Order of work
items: Trim each layer's domed top flat with a serrated knife
Layer one on the board, cut side up
Pipe a ring of buttercream around the outer edge
Spoon filling inside the ring, not over it
Next layer on, press gently, check level
Repeat, then a final layer cut side down

sections.heading: The dam
sections.body: The ring of frosting is doing real work: it holds the filling in place so it can't ooze out when the weight of the layers presses down. Without it, a fruit filling will find the edge of the cake every time.

sections.heading: Keeping it level
sections.body: Crouch down so your eye is level with the cake and look across the top. If it's leaning, nudge the top layer before you frost — once it's frosted, a lean is permanent.

how_to.counts_as_done: All layers stacked with filling between them, sitting level on the board.

steps.week_progression: Week 3 only — this is the build.

steps.title: Crumb coat and chill
steps.details: Spread a thin coat of buttercream over the whole cake — top and sides — just enough to trap the loose crumbs. Don't try to make it neat; it's meant to look rough. Then put the cake in the fridge for at least 30 minutes until that coat is firm to the touch. This is the step that makes the final coat clean, and it's the step beginners skip.

how_to.gist: Spread a thin, rough coat of frosting all over, then chill it firm.
how_to.why: A thin first coat locks the crumbs in so they can't show through the final layer. It's the difference between a smooth finish and a cake with sponge crumbs speckled through the frosting.

sections.heading: How thin
sections.body: You should still see the cake through it in places. Thin is correct — a thick crumb coat is just a first coat you'll have to fight later.

sections.heading: The chill
sections.body: At least 30 minutes in the fridge, until the frosting doesn't move when you touch it. If you're short on time, 20 minutes in the freezer works, but don't leave it longer than that.

how_to.counts_as_done: Cake covered in a thin coat and chilled firm.

steps.week_progression: Week 3 only.

steps.title: Final coat and finish
steps.details: Once the crumb coat is firm, spread the rest of the buttercream over the top and down the sides, then smooth it with a palette knife or the back of a knife, turning the cake as you go. Warm the knife under the tap and dry it if the frosting starts dragging. Finish however you like — a swirl on top, a few berries, a ring of sprinkles. Then leave it somewhere cool for an hour before anyone cuts it.

how_to.gist: Spread the final coat, smooth it with a warm knife, and finish the top.
how_to.why: This is the coat people see. Doing it on a firm crumb coat is what makes it look deliberate rather than homemade-in-a-rush.

sections.heading: Smoothing
sections.body: Load the knife, hold it at a shallow angle against the side, and turn the cake rather than moving your hand. Dip the knife in hot water and dry it whenever the frosting starts to pull — a warm knife glides, a cold one drags.

sections.heading: The top
sections.body: Bring the frosting up over the top edge and sweep inwards to the middle. A small swirl or a few berries hides more than you'd think.

sections.heading: Before cutting
sections.body: An hour somewhere cool lets the frosting set so the slices come out clean. Cutting a warm cake gives you a landslide.

how_to.counts_as_done: Cake fully frosted and finished, and left to set.

steps.week_progression: Week 3 only.

steps.title: Read the plan for your final bake and shop for it
steps.details: Weeknight slot. Next weekend is the real one — the cake you're actually making for the birthday. Decide now what flavour it is, write the full ingredient list, and buy everything. Butter out. If you're baking for a specific day, work backwards from that day and check the cake will still be good then.

how_to.gist: Choose the birthday cake's flavour, buy everything for it, put the butter out.
how_to.why: The final bake should be a repeat of something you've already done, not a new recipe you're meeting for the first time. Deciding now is what makes it a repeat.

sections.heading: Decide now
items: Which sponge — the one you've baked three times
Which filling
Which frosting
What goes on top

sections.heading: Work backwards
sections.body: If the cake is needed on a particular day, count back: bake the sponge the day before, assemble and frost the morning of, or assemble the day before and let it set overnight. Write the days down.

how_to.counts_as_done: Flavour chosen, full shopping list bought, butter out, days written down.

steps.week_progression: Week 3 only — this is the run-up to the real thing.

phases.title: The real cake
phases.focus: Bake the birthday cake end to end, cleanly, on your own timing — and keep the recipe you've built.

steps.title: Bake the birthday cake, start to finish
steps.details: The whole thing in one long session: sponge, cool, filling, frosting, stack, crumb coat, chill, final coat. Same recipes as the last three weeks, no new ones. Give yourself the full session — this takes longer than the practice bakes because you're doing all of it in one go, and rushing the chill is the one thing that ruins it.

how_to.gist: Bake, fill, stack and frost the birthday cake in one long session.
how_to.why: This is the goal. Everything before now was rehearsal for this exact sequence, and you've already done every part of it at least once.

sections.heading: The run of play
items: Sponge into the oven first thing
Make the filling while it bakes
Make the buttercream while the layers cool
Trim, stack, fill
Thin coat, then chill 30 minutes
Final coat, finish, set for an hour

sections.heading: Where people rush
sections.body: The chill. Thirty minutes in the fridge between the thin coat and the final coat is not optional — skip it and the final coat drags crumbs through and looks muddy. Use the time to wash up.

sections.heading: If something goes wrong
sections.body: A cracked layer can be trimmed flat. A split buttercream comes back with a warm bowl and more whisking. A leaning stack can be nudged before frosting. Nothing here is unfixable, and you've seen most of it already.

how_to.counts_as_done: A finished, frosted, layered cake on the board.

steps.week_progression: Week 4 only — the real bake.

steps.title: Cut it and eat it with whoever it's for
steps.details: Same day or the day after. Cut the first slice with a knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry — clean slices, no landslide. Then sit down and eat it with the person it's for. This is the point of the whole month and it's worth actually stopping for rather than eating a slice standing up over the sink.

how_to.gist: Cut the first slice with a hot knife and eat the cake with the person it's for.
how_to.why: Four weeks of practice ends in a cake that gets eaten. Stopping to actually do that is the reward the whole plan was built toward.

sections.heading: Cutting cleanly
sections.body: Hot water on the blade, wipe it dry, cut straight down and wipe the blade between slices. Cold cake cuts cleanest — if it's been out a while, ten minutes in the fridge helps.

sections.heading: The point
sections.body: You made this from flour and eggs and butter, by hand, without a stand mixer. Say so out loud when you serve it.

how_to.counts_as_done: The cake is cut and eaten with the person it was made for.

steps.week_progression: Week 4 only.

steps.title: Write the recipe out as your own
steps.details: Take your recipe card with four weeks of notes on the back and write out a clean version: the sponge, the filling, the frosting, the timings that actually worked in your oven, and the order you do things in. That card is the thing you keep — next birthday you start from it instead of from scratch.

how_to.gist: Write a clean recipe card from your four weeks of notes — your version, your oven, your timings.
how_to.why: The month's real product isn't one cake, it's a recipe that works in your kitchen. Writing it out now is what makes next year's cake a two-hour job instead of a four-week project.

sections.heading: What goes on it
items: Sponge ingredients and your actual mixing time
Your oven temperature and real bake time
Filling and frosting quantities that covered the cake
The order of assembly, in your words

sections.heading: Where to keep it
sections.body: Back on the cupboard door, next to the shelf. That's where it gets used.

how_to.counts_as_done: A clean, complete recipe card in your own words.

steps.week_progression: Week 4 only — the takeaway.

milestones.title: First sponge out of the tin in one piece
milestones.criteria: Two sponge layers baked, cooled and turned out whole, with the shelf set up and the first note written on the recipe card.

milestones.title: Buttercream that holds a peak
milestones.criteria: A bowl of hand-whisked buttercream that's smooth and holds its shape, a filling cooked and tasted alongside it, and three sponge layers wrapped and ready.

milestones.title: A stacked, frosted cake
milestones.criteria: Layers trimmed and stacked level with filling between them, a thin coat chilled firm, and a finished cake that sets cleanly before cutting.

milestones.title: The birthday cake, made by you
milestones.criteria: A layered birthday cake baked, filled, stacked and finished from scratch in one session, eaten with the person it was for, and written up as your own recipe card.

protocol.coach_notes: Four bakes, one skill each — that's the whole plan, and it's deliberately unhurried. The one thing that will decide this is the weeknight slot: twenty minutes on Wednesday reading the recipe and putting the butter out is what makes Saturday start on time, and it's the first thing people drop. If a bake goes wrong, that's not a lost week — a sunken sponge or a split buttercream is exactly the thing you needed to see once, and you'll recognise it next time. Miss a bake and the rule is simple: don't miss the next one. The rep after a miss is the one that decides whether this sticks.

sessions.goal: Read 10 minutes before bed every night for the next month.

protocol.goal_statement: Read 10 minutes in bed every night for the next month — book on the nightstand, phone out of arm's reach.

phases.title: Set the trap
phases.focus: Get the book into your hand at 11pm and the phone out of reach — this week is about placement, not pages.

steps.title: Put the book where the phone sleeps
steps.details: Before bed tonight, move the phone's charging spot to the far side of the room and put your book on the nightstand in its place. One-time setup, done once, that decides every night after it.

how_to.gist: Swap the nightstand: book on it, phone charging across the room.
how_to.why: Last time the scroll won because the phone was the thing within reach. Change what your hand finds first and the night mostly takes care of itself.

sections.heading: Do this once
items: Clear the nightstand of everything except the book and a lamp
Move the charger to the far wall — across the room, not across the bed
Put the book flat on the nightstand, cover up, where the phone used to sit
If you use the phone as an alarm, dig out a real alarm clock or set the phone face-down across the room

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: A phone within arm's reach is a phone you pick up without deciding to. Across the room, picking it up becomes a small trip you have to mean. The book, meanwhile, is already under your hand.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: If the phone ends up back on the nightstand, don't lecture yourself — just walk it back across the room before you get in. The setup is the habit; redoing it is allowed.

how_to.counts_as_done: Book on the nightstand and phone charging across the room when you get into bed.

steps.week_progression: Done once this week; re-check it any night the phone drifts back.

steps.title: Read 10 minutes in bed
steps.details: In bed around 11, book open, ten minutes. Phone stays across the room. On a wrecked night, two minutes counts — the only thing that doesn't count is zero.

how_to.gist: Ten minutes with the book open in bed — two minutes on wrecked nights.
how_to.why: Ten minutes is small enough to survive a bad night, which is most of them. The point this month isn't finishing books, it's making reading the thing you do in that slot.

sections.heading: The rep
items: Get into bed around your usual 11pm
Pick up the book before you pick up anything else
Read until ten minutes are up — a timer is fine, a chapter is fine
Phone stays across the room the whole time

sections.heading: Wrecked nights
sections.body: Tired, late, bad day — open the book and read two minutes. Two minutes still counts as the night done. Zero is the only outcome that breaks the chain, and a two-minute night keeps the slot yours.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: If you catch yourself scrolling in bed, that's information, not failure: the phone got within reach. Put it back across the room and open the book for whatever's left of the ten minutes.

how_to.counts_as_done: Book open in bed for at least two minutes, phone across the room.

steps.week_progression: Ten minutes nightly, two-minute floor on bad nights.

steps.title: Keep a book within reach all day
steps.details: Carry the book (or keep it in your bag) so the only copy isn't stranded on the nightstand. If you finish it, the next one goes on the nightstand the same day.

how_to.gist: Keep the book with you, and replace it the day you finish it.
how_to.why: The fastest way to kill this habit is to finish a book on a Tuesday and have nothing to pick up on Wednesday. A book that travels with you also gets read in waiting rooms and queues.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: The book lives in your bag or on your person during the day and returns to the nightstand at night. When you're within about 30 pages of the end, line up the next one so there's never a night with nothing to open.

sections.heading: Picking the next one
sections.body: Something you actually want to read beats something you think you should. If a book has been sitting unopened for two weeks, it's the wrong book — swap it, no guilt.

how_to.counts_as_done: Book with you during the day, and a next book ready before the current one runs out.

steps.week_progression: Same all month; the swap-the-book rule matters more as you get faster.

steps.title: Phone charges outside the bedroom
steps.details: From the moment you head to bed, the phone stays on its charger across the room — no last check in bed, no alarm-setting in bed. If you need an alarm, use a clock.

how_to.gist: Phone goes on the charger before you get in, and stays there.
how_to.why: Distance is the whole trick. A phone across the room is a phone you mostly don't pick up — and the nights you do pick it up are the nights the reading doesn't happen.

sections.heading: The routine
items: Plug the phone in across the room before you get into bed
Do your last check standing up, not lying down
Set any alarm before you leave the phone, not after you're in bed
Get in bed and reach for the book

sections.heading: The one exception
sections.body: If someone might genuinely need to reach you overnight, keep the phone across the room on loud rather than beside your head on silent. Same distance, no scrolling.

how_to.counts_as_done: Phone on the charger across the room, not in bed with you.

steps.week_progression: Same all month.

phases.title: Make it the default
phases.focus: Same ten minutes, same slot — now with a page target so the reading has somewhere to go.

steps.title: Read 10 minutes in bed
steps.details: Ten minutes nightly, phone across the room. Same slot as last week — the goal now is that you stop deciding and just do it.

how_to.gist: Ten minutes with the book open, phone across the room.
how_to.why: Week two is where the slot stops being a decision. Same time, same place, same ten minutes — the less you think about it, the more reliably it happens.

sections.heading: The rep
sections.body: In bed around 11, book open, ten minutes. Two minutes still counts on a wrecked night. Nothing about the setup changes this week — that's the point.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: One missed night is noise. The night after a miss is the one that decides whether this is a habit or a story you tell about trying — so make that one a two-minute night at minimum.

how_to.counts_as_done: Book open in bed for at least two minutes, phone across the room.

steps.week_progression: Same ten minutes; the two-minute floor still applies.

steps.title: Read at least 8 pages a night
steps.details: Roughly what ten minutes gets you in a normal paperback. If you're reading something denser, hold the ten minutes and let the pages land where they land.

how_to.gist: About 8 pages a night — roughly ten minutes of ordinary reading.
how_to.why: A page number gives the ten minutes somewhere to land, and gives you something to notice when the same ten minutes starts carrying more pages.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: Eight pages is a typical ten minutes in a normal paperback — about 250 words a page. Dense non-fiction or small print will run slower; in that case the ten minutes is the target and the pages are just a side effect.

sections.heading: Don't chase it
sections.body: If you're gripped and read twenty pages, great. If you read four and fall asleep, that's a two-minute night and it still counts. The number is a marker, not a test.

how_to.counts_as_done: Ten minutes read, or 8 pages, whichever comes first.

steps.week_progression: Hold at 8 pages; the ten minutes is the real target.

steps.title: Phone charges outside the bedroom
steps.details: Same rule as week one: phone on the charger across the room before you get in, last check done standing up.
steps.week_progression: Same all month.

steps.title: Keep a book within reach all day
steps.details: Book travels with you; the next one is on the nightstand before the current one runs out.
steps.week_progression: Same all month.

phases.title: Hold it on the hard nights
phases.focus: The habit meets real life — travel, late nights, bad days — and the rule is that the slot survives them.

steps.title: Read 10 minutes in bed
steps.details: Ten minutes nightly. This week the test is the nights that aren't normal — late home, away, exhausted. Two minutes still counts; the slot still happens.

how_to.gist: Ten minutes in bed, including on the nights that aren't normal.
how_to.why: Three weeks in, the habit is real but fragile — it's the unusual nights that decide whether it survives. Keeping the slot on a bad night is worth more than a great night's reading.

sections.heading: Away from home
sections.body: Traveling or staying somewhere else? The book comes with you and the phone still charges across the room. Same ten minutes, different nightstand.

sections.heading: Very late nights
sections.body: Home at 1am is a two-minute night, not a zero night. Open the book, read a page and a half, put it down. The chain stays intact and tomorrow is normal again.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: Miss a night and the next one is a two-minute night at minimum. One miss is noise; two in a row is how the old pattern gets back in.

how_to.counts_as_done: Book open in bed for at least two minutes, phone across the room.

steps.week_progression: Same ten minutes, but the two-minute floor gets used more — that's fine.

steps.title: Phone charges outside the bedroom
steps.details: Same rule, including away from home — charger on the far side of the room, last check standing up.

how_to.gist: Phone on the charger across the room, at home or away.
how_to.why: The nights you most want the phone in reach — tired, wired, away from home — are exactly the nights it costs you the reading.

sections.heading: The routine
items: Plug the phone in across the room
Last check standing up
Alarm set before you leave the phone
Get in bed and reach for the book

sections.heading: Away
sections.body: In a hotel or a friend's spare room, put the phone on the far side of the room and the book on the bed. Same distance, same result.

how_to.counts_as_done: Phone on the charger across the room, not in bed with you.

steps.week_progression: Same all month.

steps.title: Read at least 8 pages a night
steps.details: Same marker as last week — about ten minutes of ordinary reading. The ten minutes is the target; the pages are how you notice it getting easier.
steps.week_progression: Hold at 8 pages.

steps.title: Keep a book within reach all day
steps.details: Book with you during the day, next one lined up before the current one ends — especially before any trip.
steps.week_progression: Same all month.

phases.title: Keep it without the streak
phases.focus: The month is nearly up — the reading stays, the pressure comes off, and the setup is what carries it forward.

steps.title: Read 10 minutes in bed
steps.details: Ten minutes nightly, same slot. This week, a missed night is allowed to just be a missed night — no restart, no making up for it, just the next night as usual.

how_to.gist: Ten minutes in bed — and a missed night is just a missed night.
how_to.why: Four weeks in, the habit doesn't need a perfect record to survive. Loosening the perfection rule now is what keeps you reading in month two.

sections.heading: The rep
sections.body: Same ten minutes, same slot, phone across the room. Two minutes on a wrecked night still counts.

sections.heading: No restart rule
sections.body: If you miss a night, don't start the count over and don't try to read twenty minutes the next night to make up for it. Just read ten the next night. The habit is the setup, not the streak.

sections.heading: After this month
sections.body: Keep the nightstand arrangement exactly as it is. That one physical fact — book within reach, phone across the room — is what has been doing the work all along.

how_to.counts_as_done: Book open in bed for at least two minutes, phone across the room.

steps.week_progression: Same ten minutes; a missed night no longer resets anything.

steps.title: Phone charges outside the bedroom
steps.details: The arrangement that made the month work — keep it exactly as it is.
steps.week_progression: Same all month.

steps.title: Keep a book within reach all day
steps.details: Book with you, next one ready before this one ends. This is what keeps the nightstand from going empty after the month is over.
steps.week_progression: Same all month.

milestones.title: The nightstand swapped
milestones.criteria: Seven nights in a row where the book was on the nightstand and the phone charged across the room.

milestones.title: Ten nights of reading in a row
milestones.criteria: Ten consecutive nights with the book open in bed for at least two minutes.

milestones.title: A hard night didn't break it
milestones.criteria: At least one night this week where you were late, tired or away from home and still read — even if it was only two minutes.

milestones.title: A month of nights, and the setup that did it
milestones.criteria: Four weeks of the book on the nightstand and the phone across the room, and a book in progress you're still picking up.

protocol.coach_notes: You already know the reading isn't the hard part — the phone on the nightstand is. That's why almost every step here is about where things sit, not about wanting it more. One missed night is noise; the night after a miss is the one that decides whether this sticks, so make that one a two-minute night at minimum. Four weeks from now the arrangement should feel less like a rule and more like just how your bedroom is set up.

sessions.goal: Quit smoking over the next three months. I smoke about 10 a

protocol.goal_statement: Quit smoking for good over four months — a two-week taper down from 10 a day, a hard quit date after it, and a specific plan for the two danger zones (the after-meal cigarette and the evening drink), with nicotine replacement on board from day one.

phases.title: Count it, then start cutting
phases.focus: Know your real number, then taper it down on a fixed ladder to a quit date you can see coming.

steps.title: Count every cigarette
steps.details: For two weeks, every cigarette gets a tally — in your notes app or on a card in the pack. This is your real starting number, not a guess. Most people are surprised by it.

how_to.gist: Tally every cigarette you smoke for the next two weeks
how_to.why: You said about 10 a day, but 'about' is how tapers go wrong. Two weeks of real numbers tells us exactly what ladder to climb down — and it's the first time you'll have seen this habit written down.

sections.heading: How
sections.body: Keep a note on your phone or a folded card in the pack. One mark per cigarette, the moment you light it — not from memory at bedtime. If you forget one, mark it anyway when you remember.

sections.heading: The cap
items: 10 cigarettes a day is the ceiling for these two weeks
If you're under it, good — that's your real number
If you're over it, write the real number down and keep going

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: Your taper ladder is built from this number. Guessing high makes week one impossible; guessing low makes the quit date feel like a cliff.

how_to.counts_as_done: A tally exists for every cigarette today, and the day's total is at or under 10.

steps.week_progression: Same job both weeks — just get the honest number.

steps.title: Step the ladder down
steps.details: Week 1: no more than 8 a day. Week 2: no more than 6 a day. Cut the easiest ones first — the ones you smoke out of habit rather than want.

how_to.gist: Week 1 cap 8 a day, week 2 cap 6 a day
how_to.why: A cliff is what killed the last two attempts at week two. A ladder you can see the bottom of is a different thing entirely — you're already proving you can go without, just not all at once.

sections.heading: The ladder
items: Week 1: 8 a day maximum
Week 2: 6 a day maximum
Quit day: zero, and it stays zero

sections.heading: Which ones go
sections.body: Start with the cigarettes you don't actually enjoy — the one you light because you're standing outside anyway, the one that's just something to do with your hands. Leave the after-meal one for last; it's the hardest and it doesn't need to be first.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: Going over the cap one day doesn't reset the ladder. Write the number down, stay at the same cap tomorrow, and don't drop to zero early to 'make up for it' — that's the cold-turkey move that's already failed twice.

how_to.counts_as_done: Today's tally is at or under the week's cap.

steps.week_progression: Week 1 caps at 8; week 2 caps at 6.

steps.title: Pick your quit date and tell people
steps.details: Choose a Monday two weeks out and write it somewhere you'll see it daily. Then tell three people — one who sees you at work, one at home, one who'll actually ask you about it.

how_to.gist: Set the quit Monday and tell three people out loud
how_to.why: You've quit twice in private and relapsed twice in private. A date you can see coming plus people who know it's coming changes what week two feels like.

sections.heading: The date
sections.body: Pick a Monday that's two weeks from today. Put it in your phone calendar as an all-day event named 'Quit day', and write it on a sticky note where you keep your cigarettes.

sections.heading: Who to tell
items: One person at work who sees you step out
One person at home
One person who will genuinely ask you how it's going

sections.heading: What to say
sections.body: Keep it plain: 'I'm quitting on the 14th. I'm tapering down first. I'll probably be rough for a couple of weeks.' That's it — you're not asking permission, you're removing the option of quietly going back.

how_to.counts_as_done: The date is in your calendar and three people have heard it from you.

steps.week_progression: One-time job in week 1.

steps.title: Move the after-meal cigarette
steps.details: After every meal, get up and do something with your hands for ten minutes — dishes, a short walk, teeth brushed. The cigarette doesn't get to be the automatic next thing.

how_to.gist: Ten minutes of something else right after every meal
how_to.why: You named after-meal cigarettes as one of your two hardest moments. The cigarette isn't the craving — it's the thing that happens next. Change what happens next and the moment loses its grip.

sections.heading: The ten minutes
items: Stand up as soon as you finish eating
Dishes, a walk around the block, teeth brushed — pick one
Hands busy, mouth busy: coffee, tea, gum, water

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: If you still want one after the ten minutes, that's allowed during the taper — but it's a decision now, not an automatic reach. By quit day the answer is no, and by then the ten minutes is already a habit.

sections.heading: Why it works
sections.body: You're not fighting the urge, you're breaking the join between finishing a meal and lighting up. That join is what makes it feel like it isn't a choice.

how_to.counts_as_done: After each meal today, ten minutes passed before any cigarette — or none was smoked at all.

steps.week_progression: Same move both weeks; it's already in place before quit day.

steps.title: Write your drink-hour plan
steps.details: Write down, on paper, what the evening drink hour looks like from quit day on: what you'll drink, what's in your hand instead of a cigarette, and what you'll do when the urge hits at minute twenty.

how_to.gist: One page: what you drink, what's in your hand, what you do at the urge
how_to.why: You said evenings with a drink are the hardest, and that's the door week two walked through twice. A plan written in advance is the difference between a decision and a coin flip.

sections.heading: Three lines to write
items: What I'm drinking instead (or how many, if you're keeping the drink)
What's in my hand while I drink — gum, toothpicks, a glass of something cold
What I do when the urge peaks — a specific action, not 'resist'

sections.heading: The urge rule
sections.body: Cravings peak and fall in a few minutes. Pick one thing you'll do at that peak: step outside without cigarettes, do the dishes, call the person you told. Write the actual thing down, with a time limit — 'I'll do X for five minutes.'

sections.heading: Keep it visible
sections.body: Put the page where you drink. Not in a drawer — on the table, where the ashtray used to be.

how_to.counts_as_done: The page is written and it's sitting where you drink in the evening.

steps.week_progression: Written in week 1, tested for real from quit day.

phases.title: Quit day and the two weeks that killed it before
phases.focus: Zero cigarettes, nicotine replacement from day one, and a written response for week two instead of surprise.

steps.title: Zero cigarettes
steps.details: From your quit Monday, no cigarettes at all — not one, not a drag off someone else's. This is the line, and it's a clean one.

how_to.gist: No cigarettes at all, starting your quit Monday
how_to.why: This is the goal itself. Everything before it was the runway; everything after it is holding the line.

sections.heading: The line
sections.body: Zero means zero. Not 'a couple on a bad day', not half of one at a party. The first cigarette after a quit is the one that restarts the whole thing — that's not a scare tactic, it's just how it went the last two times.

sections.heading: If you smoke one
sections.body: It's not over. Throw the pack away, note what was happening when you lit it, and start again the same day. One cigarette is a slip; a pack is a relapse. Don't let the first turn into the second.

sections.heading: What to expect
sections.body: Days two to four are the roughest physically. It eases. Week two is the one that got you twice — that's why the next steps exist.

how_to.counts_as_done: No cigarettes today.

steps.week_progression: Zero from week 3 onward, permanently.

steps.title: Use the nicotine replacement every day
steps.details: Patch on in the morning, on clean dry skin, first thing. Gum for the sharp moments — after meals, the drink hour, work breaks. Use it on schedule, not only when you feel desperate.

how_to.gist: Patch on every morning, gum for the sharp moments
how_to.why: You've never used patches or gum — both previous attempts were cold turkey, and both died at week two. This is the piece that was missing, and it's not cheating, it's the difference between a craving and a collapse.

sections.heading: The patch
sections.body: One patch each morning on clean, dry, hairless skin — upper arm or back. Put it on before you'd normally have your first cigarette. Leave it on through the day; take it off before bed if it keeps you awake.

sections.heading: The gum
items: After every meal
At the evening drink
On work breaks, especially the ones where you'd step out
Any time an urge spikes hard

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Use it on a schedule, not as a last resort. Waiting until you're desperate means you're already losing that moment. Chew the gum slowly until it tingles, then park it against your cheek.

how_to.counts_as_done: Patch on this morning and gum used at the moments you planned.

steps.week_progression: Daily from quit day. Same patch strength through week 6.

steps.title: Plan for week two like it's coming
steps.details: Before week two starts, write down the three situations most likely to break you and one specific thing you'll do in each. Then tell the person you named at work that week two is the danger week.

how_to.gist: Name your three riskiest moments and one move for each
how_to.why: Week two has ended this twice. It's not a mystery and it's not bad luck — it's a known date on the calendar, and known dates can be planned for.

sections.heading: The three
items: The after-meal cigarette
The evening drink
The work step-out — especially if someone offers you one

sections.heading: One move each
sections.body: For each one, write the single thing you'll do instead. Not a list of options — one move. 'Walk to the far end of the car park.' 'Gum, then the dishes.' 'Say no once and change the subject.'

sections.heading: Say it out loud
sections.body: Tell the person at work: 'Week two is when I've cracked before. If you see me about to bum one, say something.' That's the whole ask.

how_to.counts_as_done: The three situations and their moves are written down, and one person knows week two is the risk.

steps.week_progression: Written at the end of week 3, live through week 4.

steps.title: Keep the after-meal ten minutes
steps.details: Same move as before, now with no cigarette at the end of it. Up from the table, hands busy for ten minutes, gum if the urge is loud.

how_to.gist: Ten minutes of something else after every meal, no cigarette after
how_to.why: This is the habit that replaces the automatic one. It's already two weeks old by now — you're not starting it, you're keeping it.

sections.heading: The move
items: Up from the table immediately
Dishes, a walk, teeth brushed
Gum if the urge is loud

sections.heading: The drink hour
sections.body: Same thing at the evening drink: your written page is on the table, the gum is within reach, and the first ten minutes are the ones that matter.

how_to.counts_as_done: Ten minutes passed after each meal and after the evening drink with no cigarette.

steps.week_progression: Unchanged — this is the replacement, and it stays.

steps.title: Bedtime by 11pm
steps.details: Lights out by 11pm. Tiredness is the quietest trigger there is — it lowers your patience for every craving and makes the evening drink do more work than it should.

how_to.gist: Lights out by 11pm, every night
how_to.why: Being short on sleep makes every urge feel bigger and every no feel harder. It's the least obvious part of quitting and one of the most reliable.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: In bed, lights out, by 11pm. Set an alarm for 10:30 that means 'start winding down', not 'get up'.

sections.heading: Why
sections.body: The evening drink hour gets longer and looser the later you stay up. An earlier night shortens the window where the hardest trigger lives.

how_to.counts_as_done: Lights out by 11pm.

steps.week_progression: Same every night.

phases.title: Steady, and step the nicotine down
phases.focus: The quit is normal now — start reducing the patch and rebuild the moments the cigarettes used to fill.

steps.title: Zero cigarettes
steps.details: Still zero. By now this is less a fight and more a fact about your day.

how_to.gist: No cigarettes, same as every day since quit day
how_to.why: The line doesn't move. What changes in this phase is everything around it.

sections.heading: The line
sections.body: Zero. The urges are thinner now and further apart — most of what's left is the habit of the moment, not the nicotine.

sections.heading: Watch for
sections.body: The 'just one, I've earned it' thought. That one arrives around now, usually on a good day. It's the same thought that ended the last two attempts.

how_to.counts_as_done: No cigarettes today.

steps.week_progression: Unchanged.

steps.title: Step the patch down
steps.details: From week 7, move to the next patch strength down. Hold it for four weeks before considering another step down. If the urges get loud, go back up — that's not failure, that's using the tool properly.

how_to.gist: Drop to the lower patch strength from week 7
how_to.why: The nicotine replacement did its job getting you through the first month. Now it comes down slowly, on a schedule, so you never hit a cliff.

sections.heading: The step down
items: Week 7: move to the next strength down
Hold it four weeks
Only step down again if the last four weeks were steady

sections.heading: If it's too much
sections.body: Go back up to the previous strength for another two weeks and try again. Stepping back up is the correct move, not a defeat — the point is to stay off cigarettes, not to win a race off the patch.

how_to.counts_as_done: Patch on this morning at the current step-down strength.

steps.week_progression: One step down at week 7, then hold.

steps.title: Fill the work break with something
steps.details: The step-out at work was one of your three moments. Five days a week, take that same break and do something with it — a walk around the block, a coffee away from the smoking spot, a call.

how_to.gist: Take the work break, but somewhere else, doing something else
how_to.why: You named stepping out at work as one of the automatic moments. The break itself is fine — it's the standing in the smoking spot that has to go.

sections.heading: The swap
items: Same time, different place
A walk, a coffee, a phone call
Not the smoking spot, and not with the people who are smoking

sections.heading: If someone offers
sections.body: One word, then move on: 'Nah, I'm off them.' Don't explain, don't negotiate. The longer the answer, the more it sounds like a question.

how_to.counts_as_done: Five work breaks this week taken somewhere other than the smoking spot.

steps.week_progression: Five a week, every week from here.

steps.title: Drink hour, no cigarette
steps.details: The evening drink stays if you want it — the cigarette doesn't. Your written page is still on the table, the gum is still within reach, and the first ten minutes still get the same move.

how_to.gist: Keep the drink if you like, keep the no-cigarette rule
how_to.why: This is your hardest moment and it's the one that ended the last two attempts. It's not going away — it's being handled.

sections.heading: The setup
sections.body: Page on the table, gum within reach, hands busy. If the drink itself is what makes the urge loud, try a different drink for a week and see if the urge follows the alcohol or the ritual.

sections.heading: The ten minutes
sections.body: Same as always: when the urge peaks, do the thing you wrote down for five to ten minutes. It passes. It always passes.

how_to.counts_as_done: Evening drink had (or skipped), no cigarette.

steps.week_progression: Unchanged — this is the permanent arrangement.

phases.title: Off the patch, and it's just your life
phases.focus: Come off the nicotine replacement, handle the odd craving without drama, and lock in the version of the evening that doesn't include cigarettes.

steps.title: Zero cigarettes
steps.details: Zero, and by now it's mostly unremarkable — which is exactly the point.

how_to.gist: No cigarettes — the last stretch of the four months
how_to.why: Four months is long enough that not smoking stops being a project and starts being who you are.

sections.heading: The line
sections.body: Zero. Cravings now are rare and short — usually tied to a drink, a stressful day, or someone else lighting up.

sections.heading: The one rule
sections.body: Not even one. Not at a wedding, not on holiday, not 'just to see'. That single cigarette is how the last two quits ended.

how_to.counts_as_done: No cigarettes today.

steps.week_progression: Unchanged.

steps.title: Come off the patch
steps.details: From week 12, step down to the lowest strength, then off entirely by week 15. If the urges spike when you stop, hold at the lowest strength a couple more weeks.

how_to.gist: Lowest patch strength from week 12, off it by week 15
how_to.why: The patch was scaffolding, not a destination. Coming off it slowly and on a schedule is how you avoid the cliff that cold turkey gave you twice.

sections.heading: The schedule
items: Week 12: lowest strength
Week 15: off entirely
If urges spike: hold at lowest for two more weeks

sections.heading: When you stop
sections.body: Expect a few restless days and some irritability. It's short and it's the last of it. Keep the gum around for the sharp moments even after the patch is gone.

how_to.counts_as_done: Patch on at the scheduled strength — or off it, if you're at week 15 or past.

steps.week_progression: Lowest strength week 12, off by week 15.

steps.title: Keep the evening as it is
steps.details: The drink, the page on the table, the gum, the ten minutes. Nothing changes here — this is the arrangement that's been working since quit day.

how_to.gist: Same evening setup: drink if you want, no cigarette, ten-minute move
how_to.why: The evening drink hour is the moment that ended this twice. It's handled now — the job is not to get bored of handling it.

sections.heading: The setup
sections.body: Page still on the table. Gum still within reach. Hands still busy. It looks the same in month four as it did in week three.

sections.heading: The trap
sections.body: The dangerous thought in this phase is 'I'm fine now, I don't need all this.' You are fine — because of all this. Keep it.

how_to.counts_as_done: Evening drink had (or skipped), no cigarette.

steps.week_progression: Unchanged.

steps.title: Spend the cigarette money
steps.details: Once a week, move what you'd have spent on cigarettes into a separate account or a jar you can see. Ten a day is real money, and watching it pile up is the reward this whole thing has been missing.

how_to.gist: Move this week's cigarette money somewhere you can see it
how_to.why: Quitting pays you back in cash every single week, and it's easy to never notice. Making it visible is the part that keeps you going when the novelty wears off.

sections.heading: The move
sections.body: Work out roughly what a week of cigarettes cost you and move that amount into a separate account, or drop it in a jar. Once a week, same day.

sections.heading: What it's for
sections.body: Give it a name — a trip, a piece of gear, something you actually want. Money with a destination is harder to spend on cigarettes.

sections.heading: The point
sections.body: Four months of not smoking is a real amount of money. Seeing it is the closest thing to a receipt for the whole thing.

how_to.counts_as_done: This week's cigarette money has been moved.

steps.week_progression: Weekly from week 12.

milestones.title: Two weeks of real numbers and a quit date on the calendar
milestones.criteria: Every day tallied, the ladder stepped down to 6 a day, the quit Monday set, and three people told.

milestones.title: Four weeks with zero cigarettes — past the week that ended it twice
milestones.criteria: No cigarettes for four straight weeks, patch on every morning, and the after-meal and drink-hour moves still running.

milestones.title: Two months smoke-free and stepping the patch down
milestones.criteria: Zero cigarettes through week 11, one patch step-down held for four weeks, and work breaks taken away from the smoking spot.

milestones.title: Four months smoke-free, off the patch
milestones.criteria: Zero cigarettes for the full four months, off nicotine replacement, and the evening drink hour handled without one.

protocol.coach_notes: You've already done the hard part twice — two weeks cold turkey, no help, no plan. What you didn't have was a runway and a tool. Now you have both: a ladder down instead of a cliff, a quit date you can see coming, patches and gum from day one, and a written answer for the evening drink. Week two is coming. You know its name now, and you've got a page on the table for it. One missed day is noise — the day after a miss is the one that decides this, so never let two in a row happen.
