protocol.goal_statement: Walk 10,000 steps a day, most days, built from a lunchtime park loop plus an after-work walk.
protocol.short_title: Walk 10,000 steps a day in 10 weeks

phases.title: Two walks, easy targets
phases.focus: Get the lunch loop and the after-work walk happening at all, at a step number that feels almost too small.

steps.title: Walk the park loop at lunch
steps.details: Leave the desk at lunch and walk the park by the office for 20 minutes. Go out the door before you decide whether you feel like it — the decision is made at 12:30, not at the desk. Keep the pace easy enough to hold a conversation.

how_to.gist: 20 minutes in the park by the office, every workday lunch.
how_to.why: This loop is the single biggest piece of your 10,000 steps — 20 minutes in the park is roughly a third of the whole gap, and it's sitting right outside your building.

sections.heading: The loop
sections.body: Walk out of the office and into the park. Any route works — one lap, two laps, or out one path and back the other. 20 minutes of steady walking, not a stroll and not a march.

sections.heading: Before you go
sections.body: Shoes stay under your desk. Lunch goes in your bag in the morning so you're not choosing between eating and walking. Leave at the same time each day so the afternoon doesn't get to vote.

sections.heading: If the day goes sideways
sections.body: A busy afternoon is the thing that kills this walk first. If you truly can't get out at lunch, the after-work walk still counts for the day — one missed loop is not a missed week.

how_to.counts_as_done: 20 minutes of walking outside the office at lunch, any route.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 20 minutes each workday.

steps.title: Walk after work
steps.details: When you get home, change shoes and go straight back out for 15 minutes before you sit down. Same route each time is fine. This is the walk that turns a decent day into a 10,000-step day.

how_to.gist: 15 minutes out the door the moment you get home, before you sit down.
how_to.why: The lunch loop alone gets you partway; this second walk is what closes the rest of the gap. Doing it before you sit down is the whole trick — once you're on the sofa, it's gone.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Home, shoes, out. No sitting first, no checking anything first. 15 minutes around the block or down the street and back.

sections.heading: Make it easy
sections.body: Leave your walking shoes by the front door. If you drive home past the park, you can also just stop there on the way and do it before you ever get in the house.

sections.heading: The floor day
sections.body: On days the lunch loop didn't happen, this walk is your floor — do it and the day still counts. On days both happen, you're already near 10,000.

how_to.counts_as_done: 15 minutes of walking after getting home, before sitting down.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 15 minutes each workday evening.

steps.title: Weekend walk
steps.details: One 30-minute walk each weekend day, somewhere you actually like being — a park, a waterfront, a neighbourhood you don't usually see. Weekends have no desk and no commute, so this is where the habit gets to feel good instead of functional.

how_to.gist: 30 minutes of walking each weekend day, somewhere you enjoy.
how_to.why: Weekends are the easiest days to hit a big number and the easiest days to hit zero. A real walk on both keeps the week from starting in a hole.

sections.heading: Where
sections.body: Pick somewhere you'd go anyway. The point is that it doesn't feel like a chore on the two days you're not at work.

sections.heading: When
sections.body: Morning works best — it's done before the day fills up. If you'd rather go after lunch, that's fine, just keep it to one walk a day.

how_to.counts_as_done: One 30-minute walk on each weekend day.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-3: 30 minutes each weekend day.

steps.title: Check your step count at the end of the day
steps.details: Look at your phone or watch before bed and see where the day landed. Weeks 1-3 the bar is 6,000 steps — 2,000 above your current 4,000 average, which the two walks cover comfortably. This is the number that creeps up over the ten weeks.

how_to.gist: Hit 6,000 steps today — 2,000 more than your current average.
how_to.why: Your baseline is about 4,000 steps a day. Asking for 10,000 in week one is how walking plans die; 6,000 is a small, real step up that the lunch loop and evening walk already cover.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: 6,000 steps a day for weeks 1-3. Your phone or watch counts them — just glance at it before bed.

sections.heading: Where it comes from
sections.body: Your normal day is about 4,000. The lunch loop adds roughly 2,000-2,500 and the evening walk another 1,500-2,000, so hitting 6,000 shouldn't need anything extra.

sections.heading: The floor day
sections.body: On a day that goes sideways, the evening walk alone still gets you close. If you land under 6,000, note it and move on — one low day doesn't undo the week.

how_to.counts_as_done: The app or your phone shows 6,000+ steps for the day.

steps.title: Shoes by the door and in your desk drawer
steps.details: One-time setup: put a pair of walking shoes by your front door tonight, and a second pair under your desk at work tomorrow. Also put a reminder on your phone for 12:25 on workdays that just says 'park'.

how_to.gist: Shoes by the front door, shoes under the desk, a 12:25 phone reminder.
how_to.why: Both walks die at the same moment — the second you have to go find something. Removing that step is worth more than any amount of good intentions.

sections.heading: Do this once
items: Walking shoes by the front door tonight
Second pair under your desk at work
Phone reminder at 12:25 on workdays, worded 'park'
Lunch packed in your bag the night before

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The gap between deciding to walk and walking should be zero steps. If the shoes are already there, the walk starts the moment you stand up.

how_to.counts_as_done: Shoes in both places and the 12:25 reminder set.

steps.week_progression: Set up once in week 1; re-check it if the walks start slipping.

phases.title: Longer loop, higher bar
phases.focus: Stretch the lunch loop to 30 minutes and lift the daily target to 7,000.

steps.title: Walk the park loop at lunch
steps.details: Same park, same time, 30 minutes instead of 20. The extra ten minutes is worth roughly 1,000 steps and is the easiest place in your day to find them.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-6: 30 minutes each workday.

steps.title: Walk after work
steps.details: 20 minutes now instead of 15, still straight after getting home and before you sit down. If you'd rather, park at the park on the drive home and walk there.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-6: 20 minutes each workday evening.

steps.title: Weekend walk
steps.details: 40 minutes each weekend day. If you want, make one of them a longer outing — a trail, a long loop, somewhere new — and keep the other short and local.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-6: 40 minutes each weekend day.

steps.title: Check your step count at the end of the day
steps.details: The bar moves to 7,000 a day for weeks 4-6. Same routine: glance at the count before bed. If you're consistently clearing 7,000 without effort, that's the signal you're ready for the next bump — not a reason to jump ahead.
steps.week_progression: 7,000/day weeks 4-6.

steps.title: One walk on a day you'd normally skip
steps.details: Once a week, pick the day you least want to walk — the busy one, the rainy one, the one where you'd rather go straight home — and do the evening walk anyway. This is the rep that decides whether the habit survives a bad week.
steps.week_progression: One deliberately hard-won walk each week from week 4 on.

phases.title: Closing the gap
phases.focus: Push the daily target to 8,000 and add small bits of movement to the desk day itself.

steps.title: Walk the park loop at lunch
steps.details: 30 minutes, same as last phase — this one's locked in now. If you're feeling good, add a second lap rather than walking faster.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 7-8: 30 minutes each workday.

steps.title: Walk after work
steps.details: 25 minutes after getting home. This walk plus the lunch loop is now most of your day's steps.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 7-8: 25 minutes each workday evening.

steps.title: Weekend walk
steps.details: 45 minutes each weekend day. These two days are now doing real work in your weekly total, so don't let them slide.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 7-8: 45 minutes each weekend day.

steps.title: Break up the desk day
steps.details: Twice during the workday — mid-morning and mid-afternoon — get up and walk for five minutes. Take the stairs, walk a corridor, go get water the long way. Two short breaks add a few hundred steps and, more importantly, stop the day from being one long sit.
steps.week_progression: Twice each workday from week 7 on.

steps.title: Check your step count at the end of the day
steps.details: 8,000 a day for weeks 7-8. You're now within a couple of thousand of the goal, and the two walks plus the desk breaks should get you there without adding anything new.
steps.week_progression: 8,000/day weeks 7-8.

phases.title: 10,000 as the normal day
phases.focus: Land on 10,000 steps most days and prove it holds when the week goes badly.

steps.title: Walk the park loop at lunch
steps.details: 35 minutes in the park each workday lunch. This is the walk that makes 10,000 possible rather than lucky.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-10: 35 minutes each workday.

steps.title: Walk after work
steps.details: 25 minutes after getting home, before you sit down. On a day the lunch loop got eaten by work, this is the walk that saves the day.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-10: 25 minutes each workday evening.

steps.title: Weekend walk
steps.details: 45 minutes each weekend day, same as last phase. Keep them.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-10: 45 minutes each weekend day.

steps.title: Break up the desk day
steps.details: Two five-minute walks during the workday, mid-morning and mid-afternoon, same as last phase. These are now part of how you work, not a special effort.
steps.week_progression: Twice each workday, weeks 9-10.

steps.title: Check your step count at the end of the day
steps.details: 10,000 steps on workdays — five days a week, not seven. Weekends you'll often clear it anyway with the 45-minute walks, but the bar is the five workdays. 'Most days' is the goal, and five out of seven is most days.
steps.week_progression: 10,000/day on workdays, weeks 9-10.

steps.title: One full week at 10,000
steps.details: In the final week, hit 10,000 on all five workdays. If a day falls short, the next day's walk is the one that matters — one short day is noise, two in a row is a pattern.
steps.week_progression: Week 10 only: five workdays at 10,000.

milestones.title: Three weeks of two walks a day
milestones.criteria: The lunch loop and the after-work walk have both happened on most workdays for three straight weeks, and the daily count is sitting at 6,000 or above.

milestones.title: 7,000 steps is your normal day
milestones.criteria: You're clearing 7,000 steps most days without having to think about it, and the lunch loop has stretched to 30 minutes.

milestones.title: 8,000 steps, and the desk day moves
milestones.criteria: Daily count is at 8,000 or above, and you're taking two short walking breaks during the workday without needing to remember to.

milestones.title: 10,000 steps is what a workday looks like
milestones.criteria: Five workdays in a row at 10,000 steps or more, with the lunch loop and the after-work walk both in place.

protocol.coach_notes: You already did the hard part — you know exactly where these steps come from, and there's a park sitting outside your office. The plan just asks you to show up at 12:30 and again when you get home, starting at a number that's barely above what you already walk. One missed day is noise. The day after a miss is the one that decides whether this sticks, so make that the day you don't negotiate with yourself.

sessions.goal: Read a lot more this year — I keep buying books and not read

protocol.goal_statement: Read 10 pages in bed at 10:30 on weeknights, phone charging in the kitchen overnight, plus one audiobook chapter on the Saturday walk

phases.title: The setup
phases.focus: Get the phone out of the bedroom and the book onto the pillow, then read ten pages on weeknights — two pages counts on the nights that go sideways.

steps.title: Phone charges in the kitchen overnight
steps.details: Every night, the phone goes on the kitchen charger before you head to bed — not on the nightstand, not in the bedroom at all. This is the move that does the work: the thing that's been winning at 10:30pm simply isn't in the room. If you use the phone as an alarm, pick up a cheap alarm clock this week so there's no reason to bring it back.

how_to.gist: Phone on the kitchen charger before you get into bed, every night.
how_to.why: You wrote this one yourself, and it's the strongest part of the plan. Reading at 10:30 only happens if the phone isn't lying there next to you — so the phone leaves the room rather than you out-willing it.

sections.heading: The move
sections.body: Before you get into bed, walk the phone to the kitchen and plug it in. Not on the nightstand, not face-down on the dresser — out of the bedroom entirely. It stays there until morning.

sections.heading: The alarm problem
items: Buy or dig out a cheap alarm clock this week
Set it on the nightstand tonight
That's the only reason the phone ever needs to be in the bedroom — remove it

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: If the phone ends up in the bedroom, plug it in across the room rather than next to the bed. Still counts, and it's better than nothing — but the kitchen is the target.

how_to.counts_as_done: The phone spent the night in the kitchen, not the bedroom.

steps.week_progression: Week 1: set up the alarm clock and start the kitchen charging tonight. Weeks 2-4: same, every night, no exceptions for weekends.

steps.title: Read 10 pages in bed at 10:30
steps.details: At 10:30 on weeknights, you're in bed with the book — ten pages before you turn the light off. The book lives on your pillow or nightstand during the day so it's the first thing your hand finds. Ten pages is roughly ten minutes; it's meant to be small enough to hit on a tired night.

how_to.gist: In bed at 10:30 with the book, ten pages before lights out.
how_to.why: This is your own number and your own time. Ten pages is deliberately modest — small enough that a bad day doesn't stop it, which is the only kind of reading target that survives past week two.

sections.heading: The setup
items: Book on the pillow or nightstand during the day
Phone already in the kitchen
In bed at 10:30, book in hand

sections.heading: The ten pages
sections.body: Read ten pages. Roughly ten minutes. Stop there if you want — the point is the ten pages, not a chapter. If you're pulled in and keep going, that's a bonus, not the requirement.

sections.heading: The floor
sections.body: On the nights work blows up and ten pages is genuinely impossible, two pages counts. Never zero. Two pages keeps the run alive and keeps you the person who reads before bed.

sections.heading: Never two in a row
sections.body: One missed night is noise. Two in a row is how last year's attempt ended. If you miss a night, the next night is the one that matters — even if it's just the two-page floor.

how_to.counts_as_done: Ten pages read in bed (two pages on a brutal night), or the night is a miss.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: ten pages, two-page floor on bad nights. Weeks 3-4: same target, but the goal is five nights out of five instead of four.

steps.title: One audiobook chapter on the Saturday walk
steps.details: On your Saturday walk, headphones in and one chapter of an audiobook. This is your second channel — it keeps the week alive when the weeknights collapse, and it's the one that survives busy stretches because the walk was happening anyway. Have the audiobook downloaded and queued before Saturday so there's no fumbling at the door.

how_to.gist: One audiobook chapter during your Saturday walk.
how_to.why: You gave yourself a backup channel, and it's a good one: the walk already happens, so the reading rides along with it. On weeks the weeknights fall apart, this is what keeps the week from being a zero.

sections.heading: Before you go
items: Audiobook downloaded and queued Friday night
Headphones charged and by the door
Chapter picked — no browsing at the door

sections.heading: The walk
sections.body: Start the chapter when you set off. One chapter is the target; if the walk runs long, let it keep playing. If the chapter ends before you're home, that's the rep done.

sections.heading: Why it's here
sections.body: This is the channel that survives a bad week. When work eats the weeknights, a Saturday chapter still means you read this week — and that's the difference between a rough week and a quit.

how_to.counts_as_done: One full chapter played during the Saturday walk.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-4: one chapter each Saturday. Keep the queue stocked so you never start the walk without something ready.

steps.title: Two pages on any night that gets away from you
steps.details: This is the floor, and it's the one addition to your plan. Last year's attempt died in week two when work got busy — not because you stopped wanting to read, but because a few missed nights turned into feeling behind, and feeling behind turned into stopping. So on the nights ten pages is genuinely impossible, two pages counts as a full rep. Never zero. Two pages keeps the run alive and keeps you the person who reads before bed.

how_to.gist: On a night that's gotten away from you, two pages still counts.
how_to.why: Your last attempt ended in week two when work got busy — the plan had no answer for the brutal night, so a few misses became a quit. This is that answer. It's a floor, not a new rule.

sections.heading: When it applies
sections.body: Late night, early morning, work blew up, you're exhausted — any night where ten pages genuinely isn't happening. Open the book and read two pages before lights out.

sections.heading: Why two
sections.body: Two pages takes about a minute. It's small enough that no night is truly impossible, which means the run never breaks. The number isn't the point on these nights — staying the person who reads before bed is.

sections.heading: The one hard rule
sections.body: Never two zeros in a row. One missed night is noise. Two in a row is how last year's attempt ended. If you miss a night, the next night is the one that decides it.

how_to.counts_as_done: Two pages read on a night where ten wasn't possible — or the night is a miss.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-4: use it freely on bad nights. The goal is that no week ever contains two zero nights in a row.

steps.title: Keep the next book within arm's reach
steps.details: Once a week, make sure the book you're reading is physically where you'll be reading it — on the pillow, on the nightstand, in the bag you take on the Saturday walk. If you're near the end, have the next one picked and waiting. You said you keep buying books and not reading them; this is the step that stops the pile from being decoration.

how_to.gist: Once a week, put the current book where you'll actually read it.
how_to.why: You told me you keep buying books and not reading them. A book in a stack across the room is a book you don't read — this step makes sure the one you're in is always within reach of the place you read.

sections.heading: The check
items: Current book on the pillow or nightstand
If you're near the end, next book picked and waiting
Saturday walk book or audiobook queued

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: Every step between you and the page is a chance to drift to something else. This one removes the step — the book is already there when you get into bed.

how_to.counts_as_done: The book you're reading is sitting where you'll read it tonight.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-4: check it once a week, ideally Sunday. Adjust as you learn where you actually read.

phases.title: Five nights out of five
phases.focus: Ten pages becomes the normal weeknight, not the good weeknight — the floor stays for the nights that go sideways.

steps.title: Phone charges in the kitchen overnight
steps.details: Same as before, and by now it should be automatic — the phone goes to the kitchen before you get into bed. If it's drifted back to the bedroom, this is the week to move it out again.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-8: every night, weekends included. If the phone has crept back into the bedroom, reset it tonight.

steps.title: Read 10 pages in bed at 10:30
steps.details: Ten pages at 10:30 on weeknights — but the target for this stretch is all five nights, not four. The two-page floor is still there for the nights that genuinely go sideways; what changes is that hitting four out of five no longer feels like a full week.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-6: five nights, floor allowed. Weeks 7-8: five nights, and aim to need the floor less than once a week.

steps.title: One audiobook chapter on the Saturday walk
steps.details: One chapter on the Saturday walk, same as before. By now you should be through a book or two this way — if the queue is empty, restock it Friday night.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-8: one chapter each Saturday. If you're finishing books faster than you're buying them, that's the problem you wanted.

steps.title: Two pages on any night that gets away from you
steps.details: The floor stays. On a night where ten pages isn't happening, two pages counts. Never two zeros in a row — that rule doesn't expire.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-8: use it when you need it, and notice how rarely you need it compared to week one.

steps.title: Pick the next book before you finish the current one
steps.details: Once a week, check where you are in the current book. If you're within a chapter or two of the end, pick the next one and put it on the nightstand. Finishing a book and having nothing waiting is the easiest way for the routine to stall for a week.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-8: weekly check. The aim is that you never have a night with nothing to read.

phases.title: Make it stick
phases.focus: The routine holds on its own through a busy stretch — and you're reading more than the ten pages because you want to, not because you have to.

steps.title: Phone charges in the kitchen overnight
steps.details: The phone stays out of the bedroom. By week nine this should be less a rule than just where the phone lives.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: every night. This is the habit that holds the rest up.

steps.title: Read 10 pages in bed at 10:30
steps.details: Ten pages at 10:30, five weeknights. Same target — what's changed is that it's no longer something you have to talk yourself into. If you're regularly reading past ten pages because you're absorbed, leave the target where it is; the ten is the floor of a good night, not the ceiling.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: five nights, ten pages minimum. Let the reading run long when it wants to.

steps.title: One audiobook chapter on the Saturday walk
steps.details: One chapter on the Saturday walk. This is the channel that carried the busy weeks — keep it running even when the weeknights are going well.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: one chapter each Saturday, every week.

steps.title: Two pages on any night that gets away from you
steps.details: The floor stays in the plan permanently. It's what kept a bad week from becoming a quit — there's no reason to drop it now that things are going well.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: keep it available. Never two zeros in a row.

steps.title: Keep the next book within arm's reach
steps.details: Once a week, make sure the current book is where you read it and the next one is picked. This is the step that keeps the pile of bought books from growing faster than the pile of read ones.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 9-12: weekly check, and take stock of how many books you've actually finished since week one.

milestones.title: Two weeks in — the week last year's attempt died
milestones.criteria: You've read on at least eight of the ten weeknights so far, the phone has slept in the kitchen every night, and you've done at least one Saturday chapter. This is the point where the last attempt ended.

milestones.title: A month of reading before bed
milestones.criteria: Four weeks of the phone charging in the kitchen, ten pages on most weeknights, and at least three Saturday chapters. You've read more in a month than you were reading in a season.

milestones.title: Five nights out of five
milestones.criteria: A full week where you read in bed every weeknight, plus the Saturday chapter — and you needed the two-page floor no more than once.

milestones.title: Reading before bed is just what you do
milestones.criteria: Twelve weeks in: the phone lives in the kitchen, ten pages happens on weeknights without a decision, and the Saturday chapter is part of the walk. Count the books you've finished since week one.

protocol.coach_notes: You wrote a better plan than most people get handed — the phone in the kitchen does more work than any amount of resolve at 10:30pm, and ten pages is small enough to survive a bad night. The one thing I added is the floor: two pages on the nights that get away from you, never two zeros in a row. That's the exact night last year's attempt died on, and now it has an answer. One missed night is noise; the night after a miss is the one that decides whether this sticks.

sessions.goal: Lose 10 lbs
I want to lose 8 kg steadily over the next 4 months.

protocol.goal_statement: Lose 8 kg over 16 weeks — about 0.5 kg a week — by holding a modest daily calorie deficit, cooking at home as you already do, walking daily, and lifting twice a week to keep muscle.

phases.title: Set the floor
phases.focus: Get the two gym days, the daily walk, the protein and the bedtime actually happening — the scale is not the point yet.

steps.title: Lift twice a week
steps.details: Two full-body sessions, Tuesday and Saturday, 40-50 minutes. Squat or leg press, a push, a pull, a hinge, and one core or carry — 3 sets of 8-12 each. Two or three light warm-up sets before the working sets. This is what decides whether the 8 kg comes off as fat or as muscle.

how_to.gist: Two full-body gym sessions, Tuesday and Saturday, 40-50 minutes each.
how_to.why: At half a kilo a week, these two sessions are the difference between losing fat and losing muscle. Two is enough — but only if they happen.

sections.heading: The session
items: Legs: squat, leg press or goblet squat — 3 sets of 8-12
Push: bench, dumbbell press or push-up variation — 3 sets of 8-12
Pull: row or lat pulldown — 3 sets of 8-12
Hinge: deadlift or hip thrust — 3 sets of 8-12
One core or carry to finish — 3 sets

sections.heading: Before working sets
sections.body: Two or three light warm-up sets on the first exercise, building up in weight. Don't count them as working sets and don't skip them — they're what makes the working sets feel good.

sections.heading: If a day slips
sections.body: Move it to the next free day that week rather than writing the week off. Two sessions in seven days is the target; which two days is negotiable.

how_to.counts_as_done: Two sessions done this week, any two days.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: keep the weights light enough that you finish every set feeling you had 2-3 reps left. Weeks 3-4: same exercises, add a little weight or a rep on each.

steps.title: Write every set down and beat last time
steps.details: During each session, note the exercise, the weight and the reps for every working set — phone notes are fine. Before your first set of each exercise, look at what you did last time and aim to add one rep or a small weight bump. Without this, the lifting is just moving things around.

how_to.gist: Log each working set, then beat last session by a rep or a small weight bump.
how_to.why: Muscle only stays when it's asked to do slightly more over time. The log is how you know what 'slightly more' means.

sections.heading: What to write
items: Exercise name
Weight used
Reps on each working set

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Open last session's note before your first set of that exercise. Add one rep, or the smallest weight jump the gym allows. If you can't beat it, match it — that still counts.

sections.heading: Where
sections.body: Phone notes, a paper notebook, whatever you'll actually have with you. It doesn't need to be tidy, it needs to exist.

how_to.counts_as_done: Every working set from both sessions is written down.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: just get the habit of writing things down. Weeks 3-4: the note from last time is what you're chasing.

steps.title: Walk 30 minutes every day
steps.details: Half an hour of walking, every day, at a pace where you could hold a conversation. One block or split into two 15s — both count. This is the quiet part of the plan and it does more than it looks like.

how_to.gist: 30 minutes of walking a day, at a pace you could talk through.
how_to.why: You already walk daily — this just puts a floor under it. It burns a real amount over a week without making you hungry the way harder cardio does.

sections.heading: The pace
sections.body: You should be able to say a full sentence without gasping. If you're breathing hard, slow down — this isn't a workout, it's volume.

sections.heading: When
items: Before work, if that's when you have a gap
At lunch, if the desk job traps you otherwise
After dinner, which also keeps you out of the kitchen

sections.heading: Splitting it
sections.body: Two 15-minute walks count as one day. Ten minutes here and there does not — 30 minutes total is the bar.

how_to.counts_as_done: 30 minutes of walking done that day, in one block or two.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: 30 minutes daily. Weeks 3-4: same 30 minutes, but on at least three days push one walk to 45.

steps.title: Hit ~150 g protein a day
steps.details: About 150 g of protein a day — roughly 1.6 g per kg at your 92 kg. A palm-sized portion of meat, fish or tofu at each meal, plus Greek yoghurt, eggs or a shake to close the gap. Protein is what keeps you full on a smaller plate and what keeps the muscle while the fat goes.

how_to.gist: About 150 g of protein a day, spread across your meals.
how_to.why: Two things at once: it keeps you full enough to hold a deficit without misery, and it's what protects your muscle while the weight comes off.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: 150 g a day. You don't need to weigh food — use your hand and a rough count.

sections.heading: Where it comes from
items: Palm-sized portion of meat, fish, eggs or tofu at each of your three meals
A pot of Greek yoghurt or cottage cheese as a snack
A scoop of whey in milk or water if the day is running short
Beans, lentils or edamame count too — just add a bit more

sections.heading: The easy check
sections.body: By evening, ask whether you had a protein portion at every meal. If two of three meals were mostly carbs, you're short — a shake fixes it in a minute.

how_to.counts_as_done: A protein portion at every meal and roughly 150 g across the day.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: get a protein portion into every meal before worrying about the total. Weeks 3-4: count roughly for a few days to calibrate what 150 g looks like.

steps.title: One plate at dinner, no seconds
steps.details: You already cook at home most nights — that's the hard part done. The change is the size of what goes on the plate: one plate, filled half with vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter starch, and no going back for more. Cook the same food, just cook a little less of it.

how_to.gist: One plate at dinner, half vegetables, and no seconds.
how_to.why: You cook at home most nights, which means you already control the food. Portion is the only lever left, and it's a smaller change than swapping the menu.

sections.heading: The plate
items: Half: vegetables or salad
A quarter: your protein
A quarter: rice, potatoes, pasta or bread

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: One plate. If you're still hungry twenty minutes later, have fruit or yoghurt — not a second plate.

sections.heading: Cooking less
sections.body: Cook roughly a quarter less than you normally would. Leftovers are fine; a second helping at the stove is what you're avoiding.

how_to.counts_as_done: Dinner was one plate, no seconds.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: just the one-plate rule. Weeks 3-4: also cut the oil and butter you cook with by about half.

steps.title: In bed by 11:30pm
steps.details: Lights out by 11:30pm, aiming for 7-8 hours. Short sleep makes you hungrier the next day and makes the deficit feel twice as hard — this is a fat-loss step, not a lifestyle lecture. Phone on the charger across the room.

how_to.gist: Lights out by 11:30pm, phone charging across the room.
how_to.why: Under-slept people eat more the next day and feel the deficit far harder. It's the cheapest thing on this list and one of the most effective.

sections.heading: The move
sections.body: Phone goes on the charger on the far side of the room at 11:00. That single change does most of the work.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: Lights out by 11:30, up at a consistent time. Seven to eight hours is the range.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: One late night is fine. Two in a row is when the hunger starts winning — treat the second night as the one that matters.

how_to.counts_as_done: Lights out by 11:30pm.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: hit 11:30 four nights out of seven. Weeks 3-4: all seven.

phases.title: Hold the line
phases.focus: The deficit is now real — the walks get longer, the lifts get heavier, and the weekly weigh-in tells you whether it's working.

steps.title: Lift twice a week
steps.details: Same two full-body sessions, now 45-60 minutes. Add a set to your main lift and keep chasing a rep or a small weight bump each session. If a third gym day ever opens up, take it — two is the floor, not the ceiling.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-6: an extra set on the main lift. Weeks 7-9: heavier working weights, reps still in the 8-12 range.

steps.title: Write every set down and beat last time
steps.details: Same logbook habit, now with a target: every main lift should be moving up over a month. If a lift has stalled twice in a row, drop the weight 10% and build back up rather than grinding the same number.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-6: beat last session on at least two lifts. Weeks 7-9: all main lifts trending up across the month.

steps.title: Walk 45 minutes every day
steps.details: The daily walk goes to 45 minutes. Same easy conversational pace. This is where the extra half-hour of burn comes from without touching your food any further.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-6: 45 minutes on weekdays, 30 is fine on weekends. Weeks 7-9: 45 minutes every day.

steps.title: Hit ~150 g protein a day
steps.details: Same 150 g target, now non-negotiable on gym days especially. On the days you lift, protein is what turns the session into kept muscle rather than just a calorie burn.
steps.week_progression: Held steady. If hunger is loud, add protein and vegetables before you add anything else.

steps.title: One plate at dinner, no seconds
steps.details: Same rule, plus one planned bigger meal a week — a dinner out, a takeaway, whatever you actually want. Planned, not drifted into. One meal a week doesn't slow this down; pretending you'll never have one is what ends plans.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-6: hold the one-plate rule six days, one free meal. Weeks 7-9: same, and keep the free meal to a single sitting rather than a whole day.

steps.title: Weigh in every Sunday morning
steps.details: Same scale, same time, first thing Sunday before eating. Write the number down. You're watching the four-week trend, not any single reading — a heavy Saturday or a salty dinner can move a day by a kilo on its own.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 5-9: expect roughly half a kilo a week off the trend. If four weeks pass with no movement, cut the dinner starch portion and add 10 minutes to the walk before changing anything bigger.

phases.title: Push through the middle
phases.focus: Weeks 10-13 are where most plans quietly die. The lifts stay heavy, the walks stay long, and the weekly number gets a stall rule attached to it.

steps.title: Lift twice a week
steps.details: Same two sessions. By now the weights should be meaningfully heavier than week one — that's the point. Keep reps in the 8-12 range and keep the warm-up sets before the working sets.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 10-13: keep adding weight or reps. If you're genuinely flat for two sessions, take one lighter week at 70% and come back.

steps.title: Write every set down and beat last time
steps.details: Same logbook. In this stretch the log is what tells you whether a flat week is a real plateau or just a bad night's sleep.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 10-13: main lifts still trending up month over month.

steps.title: Walk 45 minutes every day
steps.details: Held at 45 minutes. On the days you don't feel like it, the rule is 15 minutes minimum — you'll usually keep going once you're out.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 10-13: 45 minutes daily, with a 15-minute floor on the days you'd otherwise skip.

steps.title: Hit ~150 g protein a day
steps.details: Same target. In the middle stretch, when the deficit has been running a while, protein and sleep are the two things that keep hunger manageable.
steps.week_progression: Held steady.

steps.title: One plate at dinner, no seconds
steps.details: Same rule, one planned bigger meal a week. If the scale has been flat for three weeks, tighten the free meal to a smaller portion rather than cutting it out entirely.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 10-13: hold the rule; adjust the free meal size off the weigh-in trend.

steps.title: Weigh in every Sunday morning
steps.details: Same scale, same time. The stall rule: three consecutive weeks with no drop means you cut one thing — the dinner starch portion — and add 10 minutes to the walk. Change one thing, wait two weeks, then change another.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 10-13: keep the trend moving. Expect it to slow a little here — that's normal, not failure.

phases.title: Land it
phases.focus: The last stretch — finish the 8 kg, then make sure the habits that got you there are the ones you keep.

steps.title: Lift twice a week
steps.details: Same two sessions, right through to the end. These don't stop when the goal is hit — they're what keeps the weight off afterwards.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 14-16: hold the weights you've built up to. No need to chase new records in the last three weeks.

steps.title: Write every set down and beat last time
steps.details: Keep the log going. At the end of week 16, look back at week 1 — the difference in the numbers is the muscle you kept.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 14-16: hold or nudge up. The log is now your record of the whole 16 weeks.

steps.title: Walk 45 minutes every day
steps.details: Held at 45 minutes. This is the one to keep for life — it's the cheapest way to hold your weight once the deficit ends.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 14-16: 45 minutes daily, no exceptions needed.

steps.title: Hit ~150 g protein a day
steps.details: Same target. When you come off the deficit, protein and the two gym sessions are what stop the weight coming back.
steps.week_progression: Held steady, and keep it after week 16.

steps.title: One plate at dinner, no seconds
steps.details: Same rule. In the last three weeks, if you're at or near your target, you can add back a little starch at dinner — but keep the one-plate shape, because that's the habit doing the work.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 14-16: hold the rule; loosen the portion slightly only if the weigh-in trend says you can.

steps.title: Weigh in every Sunday morning
steps.details: Same scale, same time. Keep this one going past week 16 — a weekly number is how you catch a slow creep before it becomes 5 kg.
steps.week_progression: Weeks 14-16: watch the trend land. Then keep weighing weekly as your early-warning system.

milestones.title: Four weeks of two gym days, held
milestones.criteria: Eight lifting sessions logged in four weeks, the daily walk done most days, and the weekly weigh-in written down every Sunday.

milestones.title: Halfway, and the lifts are heavier
milestones.criteria: Every main lift is above where it started in week 1, and the four-week weigh-in trend is heading down at roughly half a kilo a week.

milestones.title: Through the stretch most plans don't survive
milestones.criteria: Thirteen weeks in, still lifting twice a week, still walking daily, and the weigh-in trend still moving down.

milestones.title: 8 kg down, muscle kept
milestones.criteria: The Sunday weigh-in trend is about 8 kg below where you started, and your main lifts are heavier than week 1 — the weight came off as fat, not muscle.

protocol.coach_notes: You already cook at home most nights, which is the single biggest lever in this whole plan — most people fail this goal at the takeout menu and you're not starting there. The two gym days are the floor, not a buffer: at half a kilo a week they're what decides whether the weight you lose is fat or muscle, so treat them as fixed and let everything else move around them. One missed day is noise; the day after a miss is the one that decides the habit, so never let two go by in a row.

sessions.goal: Get to bed by 11pm on weeknights for a month. I usually drif

protocol.goal_statement: Lights out by 11pm on weeknights for the next four weeks — phone charging outside the bedroom, with a 10:15pm sofa-to-bed handoff.

phases.title: Move the phone, move the night
phases.focus: Get the charger out of the bedroom and make the 10:15 sofa-to-bed handoff happen every weeknight. Nothing else changes yet.

steps.title: Set up the charging spot outside the bedroom
steps.details: One-time setup: pick the spot where the phone will live overnight — kitchen counter, hallway table, living room — and put the charger and cable there tonight. Then walk the bedroom and remove every other charger, cable and power strip, so there is nothing to plug into next to the bed.

how_to.gist: Move the charger out of the bedroom and clear every other one out of there.
how_to.why: The charger next to your pillow is what turns a 10pm sofa drift into a 1am scroll. You can't out-will a phone within arm's reach — so the phone sleeps somewhere else and the question never comes up.

sections.heading: Pick the spot
sections.body: Kitchen counter, hallway table, wherever you'll walk past in the morning. Somewhere that is not the bedroom and not the sofa.

sections.heading: Clear the bedroom
items: Charger and cable moved to the new spot
Any spare cable or power strip out of the bedroom
Nothing on the nightstand that plugs in
Phone goes to the new spot when you head for bed

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: If the phone is in the bedroom, the night is already lost. The charger's location decides this more than your discipline does.

how_to.counts_as_done: The charger is set up outside the bedroom and there is nothing left in the bedroom to plug a phone into.

steps.week_progression: One-time job — done once and it holds for the whole month.

steps.title: Off the sofa at 10:15
steps.details: At 10:15 on a weeknight, stand up off the sofa and start the wind-down: teeth, face, whatever your routine is, then into bed. The sofa is where the drift starts, so 10:15 is the real bedtime — 11pm is just when the lights go off.

how_to.gist: Stand up off the sofa at 10:15 and start getting ready for bed.
how_to.why: You told me the night starts on the sofa around 10 and drifts from there. If you're still sitting at 10:45, 11pm is already gone — so the handoff time is the thing you actually control.

sections.heading: The handoff
sections.body: 10:15, weeknights. Stand up. The sofa is done for the night — no "one more episode," no "just finishing this."

sections.heading: Then what
items: Phone goes to its charging spot on the way past
Teeth, face, whatever your routine is
Into bed
Lights out by 11

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: Miss the 10:15 and you can still win the night — as long as the phone ends up in the other room. The handoff is the goal; the phone's location is the floor.

how_to.counts_as_done: You were off the sofa and heading to bed by 10:15 on a weeknight.

steps.week_progression: Same time every weeknight all month. Week one is about hitting it at all, not hitting it perfectly.

steps.title: Phone in its spot before you get into bed
steps.details: The phone goes to the charging spot on the way to the bedroom — not after you're settled, not "in a minute." Once you're in bed, the phone is already in another room and the night is decided.

how_to.gist: Drop the phone at its charging spot on your way to bed, every weeknight.
how_to.why: Scrolling in bed is the last link in the chain you described. Cut it at the door and there's nothing to reach for at 11:30.

sections.heading: The move
sections.body: Walking toward the bedroom, phone goes down at the charging spot. Same motion every night, so it stops being a decision.

sections.heading: Why before, not after
sections.body: If you carry it in "just to check one thing," it stays. The phone never crosses the bedroom doorway.

sections.heading: The one exception
sections.body: If you use the phone as your alarm, get a cheap alarm clock this week so the phone has no reason to be in there.

how_to.counts_as_done: The phone spent the night at its charging spot, not in the bedroom.

steps.week_progression: Every weeknight, all month. This is the step that carries the whole plan.

steps.title: Lights out by 11pm
steps.details: In bed with the lights off by 11pm on weeknights. If you're in bed at 10:40 and asleep by 10:50, even better — 11 is the ceiling, not the target.

how_to.gist: Lights off by 11pm on weeknights.
how_to.why: You're asleep near 1am now and up at 6:30. Two hours back is the whole point of the month — and it only counts if the lights actually go off.

sections.heading: The line
sections.body: 11pm, weeknights. Lights off, in bed. Not "heading up," not "almost done" — off.

sections.heading: The nights that count
sections.body: Tuesday and Wednesday are where bedtime plans go to die. Monday is easy because it's new; by midweek the sofa is comfortable again. Those are the two nights to protect.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: One late night is noise. Two in a row is how the old pattern comes back — so the night after a miss is the one that matters most.

how_to.counts_as_done: Lights were off and you were in bed by 11pm on a weeknight.

steps.week_progression: Same 11pm line every weeknight for the month.

steps.title: Same wake time, weekends included
steps.details: Up at 6:30 on weeknights as you already are — and no more than an hour later on Saturday and Sunday. Sleeping until 10 on Sunday is what makes Monday night impossible.

how_to.gist: Keep your 6:30 wake time, and don't sleep in more than an hour on weekends.
how_to.why: A fixed wake time is what pulls your whole night earlier. If you sleep until 10 on Sunday, your body isn't tired at 11 on Monday — and week one falls apart on day one.

sections.heading: Weeknights
sections.body: 6:30, as you already do. Nothing changes here — this is the anchor holding the rest of it in place.

sections.heading: Weekends
sections.body: No more than an hour past 6:30. 7:30 is fine. 10 is not, because it costs you Monday.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The wake time sets when you get sleepy. Move it around and the 11pm line moves with it.

how_to.counts_as_done: You were up within an hour of 6:30, every day of the week.

steps.week_progression: Same all month. This is the piece that makes 11pm feel natural instead of forced.

steps.title: Bright light within 30 minutes of waking
steps.details: Within half an hour of getting up, get 10 minutes of real daylight — step outside, walk to the end of the street, or sit by a window with the curtains open. Coffee outside counts. This is what tells your body the day has started.

how_to.gist: Get 10 minutes of real daylight within half an hour of waking up.
how_to.why: Morning light is the strongest thing you can do to make yourself sleepy earlier at night. It's the other half of the 11pm line — you're not just cutting the night short, you're moving the whole clock.

sections.heading: How
items: Within 30 minutes of getting up
Step outside, or sit right at an open window
10 minutes, no sunglasses
Coffee or breakfast outside is the easiest version

sections.heading: Why outside
sections.body: Indoor light is far weaker than daylight, even on a grey morning. A cloudy day outside still beats the brightest room in the house.

sections.heading: If you miss it
sections.body: Get it whenever you can that morning. Later is worse than early, but later beats nothing.

how_to.counts_as_done: 10 minutes of daylight within half an hour of waking.

steps.week_progression: Daily, all month. Easiest version: take your morning coffee outside.

phases.title: Hold the line on the boring nights
phases.focus: The setup is done — now it's about Tuesday and Wednesday, when the sofa wins. Same times, but the phone stays out of the bedroom even on the nights you blow the handoff.

steps.title: Off the sofa at 10:15
steps.details: Same handoff as last week. This week, notice which night it's hardest — for most people it's Tuesday or Wednesday — and treat that night as the one that decides the week.
steps.week_progression: Same 10:15 time. The new part is knowing in advance which night will fight you.

steps.title: Phone in its spot before you get into bed
steps.details: The phone goes to the charging spot on the way to the bedroom. If you blew the 10:15 handoff, this still happens — a late night with the phone in the other room is a much smaller loss than a late night with it in your hand.
steps.week_progression: Unchanged, and now it's the step that saves the nights the handoff doesn't.

steps.title: Lights out by 11pm
steps.details: In bed, lights off, by 11pm on weeknights. Aim to be in bed by 10:45 so 11 is a ceiling you never test.

protocol.coach_notes: You already knew where this leaked — sofa at 10, phone at the bedside — which is more than most people can tell me. So this plan doesn't ask you to resist anything; it just moves the charger and puts a time on the sofa. The 10:15 handoff is the real bedtime, and the phone's location is the floor: even on a night you blow the handoff, if the phone sleeps in the other room you still won. One missed night is noise. The night after a miss is the one that decides whether this was a month-long project or just how you go to bed now.

sessions.goal: Do 30 push-ups in a row within 8 weeks. I can do about 8 rig

protocol.goal_statement: Build from ~8 clean push-ups to 30 unbroken push-ups in 8 weeks, training 4 mornings a week at home.

phases.title: Build the base
phases.focus: Four short morning sessions that stop one rep before your form goes — volume comes from more sets, not from grinding.

steps.title: Morning push-up session
steps.details: Four mornings a week, first thing. Five sets of 4-5 clean reps, resting 60-90 seconds between sets. Every set stops at the last rep you can do with a straight body and full lockout — never the last rep you can force. Two light warm-up sets of 5 before the working sets. Takes about 10 minutes.

how_to.gist: 5 sets of 4-5 clean reps, 60-90 seconds rest, first thing in the morning.
how_to.why: Your 8 dies on form, not strength — so every set here stops while the reps still look right. That's what makes the number grow instead of stalling.

sections.heading: The week
items: Mon — 5 sets of 4-5
Tue — 5 sets of 4-5
Thu — 5 sets of 4-5
Fri — 5 sets of 4-5

sections.heading: Before working sets
sections.body: Two light warm-up sets of 5, easy pace, just to wake the shoulders up. Then rest a minute before your first real set.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Stop each set at the last rep where your body stayed straight and your arms locked out at the top. If rep 5 gets wobbly, the set was 4. Rest 60-90 seconds between sets — the rest is part of the work, not a delay.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: Missed a morning? Do the session the next morning and carry on. Two missed mornings in a row is the only thing that actually costs you.

how_to.counts_as_done: All 5 sets done that morning, each one stopped at the last clean rep.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 1-2: 5 sets of 4-5. Week 3: 5 sets of 5-6 as the reps start feeling easy.

steps.title: Write down every set
steps.details: Right after each morning session, note the reps you got on each set in your phone. Next session, beat one set by a single rep. That one rep is the whole engine of this plan — nothing else makes the number move.

how_to.gist: Note each set's reps after the session; beat one set by a rep next time.
how_to.why: Push-up numbers don't drift upward on their own. Seeing last session's numbers in front of you is what turns 'do some push-ups' into a target you can actually beat.

sections.heading: What to write
sections.body: Five numbers, one per set, in your phone notes. That's it — no app, no spreadsheet.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Before each session, look at the last one. Beat any single set by one rep. If you can't beat any of them, repeat the session exactly as it was — that's a normal week, not a failure.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The reps you can do are set by what you did last time. Without the numbers written down, you'll repeat the same session for eight weeks and wonder why nothing changed.

how_to.counts_as_done: Five numbers written down after the session.

steps.week_progression: Same habit all eight weeks — it's the one thing that never changes.

steps.title: Hit ~150 g protein
steps.details: Roughly 150 g of protein across the day — a palm-sized portion at each of your three meals, plus a shake or a tub of Greek yogurt if you're short. Muscle repairs on protein, and four mornings of push-ups a week is real muscle work.

how_to.gist: Hit ~150 g of protein across the day, spread over your meals.
how_to.why: Four mornings of push-ups a week is real muscle work, and muscle rebuilds on protein. It's the cheapest thing you can do to make the reps come faster.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: About 150 g of protein a day, spread over three meals. A palm-sized portion at each meal gets you most of the way there.

sections.heading: Easy adds
items: Eggs at breakfast
Greek yogurt as a snack
Chicken, fish or beans at dinner
A shake or a glass of milk if you're short

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Don't count grams at the table. If every meal had a real protein portion and you topped up once, the day is done.

how_to.counts_as_done: ~150 g of protein eaten that day.

steps.week_progression: Same target all eight weeks.

steps.title: Lights out by 11pm
steps.details: In bed with the lights off by 11pm, seven nights a week. Seven to nine hours of sleep is where the reps you did this morning actually turn into strength. Set an alarm for 10:30pm to start winding down.

how_to.gist: Lights off by 11pm, seven nights a week.
how_to.why: The morning sessions are what stress the muscle; sleep is when it rebuilds stronger. Skip it and the same session stops paying you.

sections.heading: The setup
sections.body: Set a 10:30pm alarm called 'wind down'. Phone on the charger across the room when you get in. Lights off by 11.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: Seven to nine hours. If you're up at 6:30 for the session, 11pm is the latest that works.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: One late night won't hurt you. Do the morning session anyway, even if it's short — skipping it makes a bad night into a lost week.

how_to.counts_as_done: Lights off by 11pm.

steps.week_progression: Same bedtime all eight weeks.

steps.title: One easy walk
steps.details: A 20-minute walk at some point in the day, any pace, any time. It keeps your shoulders and upper back loose between sessions and gives the recovery a nudge without adding any strain.

how_to.gist: A 20-minute walk, any time of day, any pace.
how_to.why: Four mornings of pressing tightens the shoulders and upper back. A daily walk keeps them loose so the next session doesn't start stiff.

sections.heading: When
sections.body: Any time that fits — after dinner is easiest to keep. It doesn't need to be fast or far.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Twenty minutes of walking, done in one go or split into two tens. If you're already walking the dog or commuting on foot, that counts.

how_to.counts_as_done: 20 minutes of walking logged.

steps.week_progression: Same all eight weeks.

phases.title: Add volume
phases.focus: More sets, more reps per set — the same four mornings, doing noticeably more work.

steps.title: Morning push-up session
steps.details: Same four mornings, bigger session: six sets of 6-8 clean reps, 90 seconds rest between sets. Still stopping at the last rep with a straight body and full lockout. Two light warm-up sets of 5 first. About 15 minutes.

how_to.gist: 6 sets of 6-8 clean reps, 90 seconds rest, four mornings.
how_to.why: Your max is climbing, so the sessions climb with it — more sets and more reps per set, still stopping before form goes.

sections.heading: The week
items: Mon — 6 sets of 6-8
Tue — 6 sets of 6-8
Thu — 6 sets of 6-8
Fri — 6 sets of 6-8

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: 90 seconds rest between sets now — the sets are longer and you need the full recovery to keep them clean. Last clean rep ends every set.

sections.heading: If a set drops
sections.body: If set 5 or 6 falls below 6 reps, that's your signal the rest was too short or the day was too heavy. Add 30 seconds rest next time before you add reps.

how_to.counts_as_done: All 6 sets done, each stopped at the last clean rep.

steps.week_progression: Weeks 4-5: 6 sets of 6-8. Week 6: 6 sets of 8-10.

steps.title: Write down every set
steps.details: Same habit, bigger numbers: note all six sets after each session and beat one set by a rep next time. This is what tells you whether the extra volume is actually landing.

how_to.gist: Log all six sets; beat one set by a rep next session.
how_to.why: With six sets a session, the numbers are the only way to tell a good week from a flat one.

sections.heading: What to write
sections.body: Six numbers in your phone notes after each session.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Beat any one set by a rep next time. If nothing moves for two sessions in a row, add a seventh set rather than pushing sets to failure.

how_to.counts_as_done: Six numbers written down.

steps.week_progression: Same habit.

steps.title: Hit ~150 g protein

how_to.gist: Hit ~150 g of protein across the day.
how_to.why: The sessions got bigger, so the repair bill got bigger too. Same target, more important now.

sections.heading: The target
sections.body: About 150 g a day across three meals — a palm-sized portion each time, plus a shake or yogurt if you're short.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: ~150 g of protein eaten. That's the whole check.

how_to.counts_as_done: ~150 g of protein eaten that day.

steps.week_progression: Same target.

steps.title: Lights out by 11pm
steps.details: In bed, lights off, by 11pm. Seven to nine hours. The heavier sessions in this phase need the recovery more than the early ones did.

how_to.gist: Lights off by 11pm, seven nights a week.
how_to.why: Bigger sessions, bigger recovery need. This is the step that keeps the volume from turning into soreness.

sections.heading: The setup
sections.body: 10:30pm wind-down alarm, phone across the room, lights off by 11.

sections.heading: If you slip
sections.body: Do the morning session anyway, even shortened. The rep after a bad night is the one that matters.

how_to.counts_as_done: Lights off by 11pm.

steps.week_progression: Same bedtime.

steps.title: One easy walk
steps.details: Keep the 20-minute daily walk. It matters more now — the extra sets tighten the shoulders and upper back, and walking keeps them moving.

how_to.gist: A 20-minute walk, any time, any pace.
how_to.why: More sets means tighter shoulders. The walk is the cheapest way to keep them loose between mornings.

sections.heading: When
sections.body: Any time that fits. After dinner is easiest to keep.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Twenty minutes, one go or two tens.

how_to.counts_as_done: 20 minutes of walking logged.

steps.week_progression: Same all phase.

phases.title: Test and peak
phases.focus: Two max tests, a lighter week before each, and the final run at 30.

steps.title: Morning push-up session
steps.details: Week 7: six sets of 8-10 clean reps, 90 seconds rest. Week 8: drop to three easy sets of 6 on Monday and Tuesday only — then rest the shoulders completely until test day. Two light warm-up sets of 5 before working sets.

how_to.gist: Week 7: 6 sets of 8-10. Week 8: taper to 3 easy sets, then rest.
how_to.why: You can't test a max on tired shoulders. Week 7 builds, week 8 backs off so the test shows what you actually have.

sections.heading: Week 7
sections.body: Six sets of 8-10 clean reps, 90 seconds rest, four mornings. Last clean rep ends each set.

sections.heading: Week 8
items: Mon — 3 easy sets of 6
Tue — 3 easy sets of 6
Thu — rest, no push-ups
Fri — rest, no push-ups

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Nothing in week 8 should feel hard. If a set feels like work, you're doing too much for a taper week.

how_to.counts_as_done: The session as written for that day of week 7 or 8.

steps.week_progression: Week 7 heavy, week 8 tapered to nothing by test day.

steps.title: Max push-up test
steps.details: Two tests only: Saturday of week 7 and Saturday of week 8. One all-out set, counted by someone watching or filmed on your phone so you can't fudge the last few. Stop when your body stops being straight — that's the number. Week 7 tells you where you are; week 8 is the one that counts.

how_to.gist: One all-out set on Saturday, filmed or watched, stopping when form goes.
how_to.why: This is the only place the number gets tested — twice in eight weeks. Everything else is training, so the test stays honest.

sections.heading: When
items: Week 7 — Saturday
Week 8 — Saturday

sections.heading: How
sections.body: Warm up with 5 easy reps, rest two minutes, then one set to the limit. Film it on your phone or have someone count. Stop the moment your hips sag or your arms don't lock out — that rep doesn't count.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: No retests, no 'best of three'. One set, one number, written down.

how_to.counts_as_done: One filmed or watched all-out set, number written down.

steps.week_progression: Week 7 test is a checkpoint; week 8 test is the goal.

steps.title: Write down every set
steps.details: Keep logging the training sets through week 7. In week 8 you're tapering, so the log matters less — just note the two test numbers.

how_to.gist: Log week 7's sets and both test numbers.
how_to.why: The log is how you'll know what to start from if you push past 30 next time.

sections.heading: What to write
sections.body: Week 7: six numbers per session. Week 8: just the Saturday test number.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: Write it down the same day. Numbers remembered later are numbers guessed.

how_to.counts_as_done: Sets logged in week 7 and both test numbers written down.

steps.week_progression: Logging winds down with the taper.

steps.title: Lights out by 11pm
steps.details: Same bedtime, and it matters most the night before each test. A full night's sleep before Saturday is worth a couple of reps.

how_to.gist: Lights off by 11pm, especially the night before a test.
how_to.why: The Friday night before each test is the single highest-value night of sleep in the whole plan.

sections.heading: The setup
sections.body: 10:30pm wind-down alarm, phone across the room, lights off by 11.

sections.heading: Test weeks
sections.body: Friday night before a Saturday test — treat it like the most important night of the week.

how_to.counts_as_done: Lights off by 11pm.

how_to.gist: Hit ~150 g of protein across the day.
how_to.why: Keeps the strength you built through the taper instead of letting it drift in the last two weeks.

sections.heading: The target

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: ~150 g of protein eaten.
